result.question: Design-time accessibility for digital interfaces in 2026 — what must be DECIDED at concept and design time rather than checked after a build: (1) WCAG 2.2's new success criteria over 2.1 (2.5.8 target size minimum, 2.5.7 dragging movements, 2.4.11/2.4.12 focus not obscured, 3.2.6 consistent help, 3.3.7 redundant entry, 3.3.8 accessible authentication) and what each demands of a designer specifically; (2) status and timeline of WCAG 3.0 / Silver; (3) the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide — which patterns are design decisions, and "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" with concrete cases where ARIA is the wrong answer; (4) focus management on route change and view transitions in SPAs; (5) live regions / aria-live for async results and their screen-reader failure modes; (6) accessible names for custom controls; (7) legal drivers and enforcement state — European Accessibility Act (applicable June 2025), US DOJ ADA Title II web rule and its deadlines, Section 508, EN 301 549; (8) how all of this differs for native iOS (VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, traits) and native Android (TalkBack, accessibility services) versus the web. Prioritize primary sources: W3C, WAI, WebAIM, Apple HIG, Android docs, EU and DOJ official text.
result.summary: Split along the question's own seams: normative spec text (the 2.2 criteria as designer decisions), the forward-looking standard (WCAG 3.0/Silver status), practitioner implementation mechanics (ARIA APG, SPA focus, live regions, accessible names), the legal/enforcement layer (EAA, DOJ Title II, 508, EN 301 549), and the native-vs-web platform divergence. Each angle targets a different primary-source family — W3C/WAI vs WebAIM/practitioner vs EU/DOJ official text vs Apple/Google developer docs — so results complement rather than overlap.

angles.label: broad/primary — normative spec text
angles.query: WCAG 2.2 new success criteria Understanding documents site:w3.org target size minimum 2.5.8 dragging movements 2.5.7 focus not obscured 2.4.11 2.4.12 consistent help 3.2.6 redundant entry 3.3.7 accessible authentication 3.3.8
angles.rationale: Anchors the answer in W3C's own Understanding/Techniques pages, which state each criterion's intent, exceptions (the 24px spacing exception for 2.5.8, the cognitive function test for 3.3.8) and the design-time decisions each forces.

angles.label: standards roadmap / future state
angles.query: WCAG 3.0 Silver working draft status 2026 W3C AG Working Group conformance model outcomes assertions timeline when will it become a W3C Recommendation
angles.rationale: Establishes what is actually stable to design against now versus speculative — WCAG 3.0's exploratory status, its outcomes/assertions conformance model, and realistic timeline, so designers do not build against a moving target.

angles.label: practitioner/implementation mechanics
angles.query: ARIA Authoring Practices Guide patterns "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" aria-live failure modes NVDA JAWS VoiceOver single page app route change focus management accessible name computation WebAIM
angles.rationale: Covers the hands-on subtopics — APG patterns as design decisions, when ARIA is the wrong answer, live-region flakiness across screen readers, accessible names for custom controls, and SPA/view-transition focus — from WAI-ARIA APG plus practitioner sources like WebAIM and Adrian Roselli.

angles.label: legal / regulatory enforcement state
angles.query: European Accessibility Act enforcement since June 2025 DOJ ADA Title II web accessibility final rule compliance deadline April 2026 2027 Section 508 EN 301 549 official text current status
angles.rationale: Pulls the official EU Directive 2019/882, DOJ's 28 CFR Part 35 final rule with its population-tiered deadlines, Section508.gov, and ETSI EN 301 549 — the actual legal drivers and what enforcement has looked like since the EAA became applicable.

angles.label: native platform divergence — iOS vs Android vs web
angles.query: Apple Human Interface Guidelines accessibility VoiceOver accessibility traits Dynamic Type 44pt tap target versus Android TalkBack accessibility services 48dp touch target contentDescription design guidance
angles.rationale: Surfaces the platform-specific primary docs (Apple HIG accessibility, developer.android.com accessibility) to show where native semantics, trait systems, text-scaling requirements and touch-target minimums diverge from WCAG's web-shaped assumptions.

results.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 — W3C Recommendation
results.snippet: The normative standard itself (W3C Recommendation, 5 Oct 2023; 87 success criteria). Contains the verbatim requirement text and definitions for every criterion in the question, including the ones with no separate deep-dive below — 3.2.6 Consistent Help (Level A: help mechanisms repeated across pages must appear in the same relative order), 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A: previously-entered info is auto-populated or selectable, exceptions for re-entry being essential, security, or expired validity), and 2.5.7 Dragging Movements. Also the authoritative source for the normative definitions that carry the real design constraints: 'cognitive function test', 'essential', 'single pointer', and 'target'. Use this for exact wording; use the Understanding pages for intent.

results.title: Understanding WCAG 2.2 — WAI (index of all Understanding documents)
results.snippet: The hub linking every per-criterion Understanding page — each states Intent, Benefits, Examples, and the exceptions, which is where the design-time decisions actually live. Non-normative but authored by the AG Working Group, so it is the closest thing to official interpretation. Direct children relevant here: dragging-movements.html (2.5.7 — every drag interaction needs a single-pointer alternative such as tap-to-select-then-tap-to-place, or up/down buttons beside a slider; scope is 'grab and move', so path-based gestures are 2.5.1's problem, not 2.5.7's), consistent-help.html (3.2.6), redundant-entry.html (3.3.7), plus the target-size, authentication and focus pages listed separately. Also links the Failure techniques F108 (no non-dragging alternative), F109 (blocking paste/autofill of passwords) and F110 (sticky header/footer hiding focus).

results.title: What's New in WCAG 2.2 — W3C WAI
results.snippet: The canonical delta over WCAG 2.1: nine added criteria — 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum, AA), 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced, AAA), 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA), 2.5.8 Target Size Minimum (AA), 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A), 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A), 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication Minimum (AA), 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication Enhanced (AAA) — and one removal, 4.1.1 Parsing, deleted because browsers now handle malformed markup. Note the level split: 3.2.6 and 3.3.7 are Level A, so they land inside every legal baseline that references 'WCAG 2.2 AA'. Confirms the 5 October 2023 Recommendation date.

results.title: Understanding Success Criterion 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum)
results.snippet: The single most design-time-binding of the new criteria. Normative floor is 24×24 CSS px for pointer targets, with five exceptions — Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential. The Spacing exception is the one designers actually build to and it is widely misread: an undersized target passes only if a 24 CSS px *diameter* circle centred on its bounding box does not intersect another target or another undersized target's circle. That makes it a spacing-token decision (effectively 24px pitch between adjacent hit areas), not a component-size decision, and it settles dense toolbars, icon-button rows, table row actions and calendar grids at wireframe stage. 'Inline' exempts links inside running text; 'User Agent Control' exempts unstyled native controls — restyling them forfeits the exemption.

results.title: Understanding Success Criterion 3.3.8: Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
results.snippet: Requires at least one path through authentication with no cognitive function test (remembering, transcribing, puzzle-solving) — and every step of a multi-factor flow must comply, not just the first. Passes: allowing paste and password-manager autofill into password and one-time-code fields, magic links, WebAuthn/passkeys, email/SMS codes that can be copied. Fails: blocking paste on a 2FA field, 'enter characters 2, 5 and 7 of your memorable word', image-transcription CAPTCHA, memorised swipe patterns. The 'object recognition' and 'personal content' exceptions are narrow. The paired failure technique F109 covers preventing password or code re-entry in the same format. This is an information-architecture decision about the login flow, unrecoverable by post-build remediation.

results.title: Understanding Success Criterion 2.4.11: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
results.snippet: Level AA: when a component receives keyboard focus it must not be *entirely* hidden by author-created content — the AAA sibling 2.4.12 tightens this to not even partially hidden. The named culprits are sticky headers, sticky footers, cookie banners and non-modal dialogs, i.e. layout patterns chosen in the comp, not bugs found in QA. Documented remedies are design decisions too: make the banner modal so it must be dismissed, use scroll-padding so sticky chrome never overlaps the scrolled-to element, or close the notification on focus loss. Failure technique F110 is the sticky-header/footer case. Pair with 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA) for focus-indicator contrast and size specs.

results.title: Read Me First | ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) | W3C WAI
results.snippet: Primary source for the two principles that make ARIA a DESIGN-time decision, not a build-time patch. (1) "A role is a promise" — applying role="button" to a div is a commitment that you have hand-written the keyboard interactions the role implies; ARIA roles never grant browser keyboard behavior or styling, so choosing a custom widget in a mockup is implicitly committing engineering budget to a full keyboard model. (2) ARIA can "cloak and enhance" — it overrides native semantics, so wrong ARIA actively misrepresents the UI to AT rather than merely failing to help. This is the canonical W3C anchor for the 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' rule and the gate you should pass before adopting any APG pattern (combobox, tabs, treegrid, disclosure, etc.). Directly serves question part (3).

results.title: Live Region Support — Adrian Roselli (January 14, 2026)
results.snippet: The most current cross-screen-reader live-region test matrix available (published 14 Jan 2026). Roselli tested five notification mechanisms — aria-live="polite", aria-live="assertive", role="alert", the native <output> element, and dynamically-changed aria-describedby — across JAWS, NVDA, Narrator, VoiceOver (macOS + iOS), Orca, and TalkBack. Documented failure modes: role="alert" does NOT prepend the "alert" announcement in most combinations (so the role buys you nothing semantically over aria-live="assertive"); polite regions sometimes announce as assertive, notably VoiceOver on macOS, interrupting the user; dynamic description changes silently fail to announce in newer browser versions. Only consistent behavior across every combo: hidden regions correctly suppress announcements. Essential for question part (5) — it shows async-result announcements cannot be assumed to work and must be designed with a fallback (focus move, visible status text) rather than trusted.

results.title: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions | APG | W3C WAI
results.snippet: The APG's normative-adjacent practice page for question part (6): accessible names for custom controls. Sets the naming priority order designers and devs must follow — prefer a visible, on-screen label referenced via aria-labelledby; fall back to aria-label only when no visible text exists; never use aria-label to contradict visible text (which breaks WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.3 Label in Name and voice-control users). Also covers when a description (aria-describedby) is appropriate versus a name, and which roles actually support naming from content. This is a design-time decision because whether a control has a visible label at all is a layout/comp choice — icon-only buttons and placeholder-as-label patterns are the two most common naming failures and both originate in the design file, not the code.

results.title: WebAIM: Decoding Label and Name for Accessibility
results.snippet: WebAIM's practitioner walkthrough of the Accessible Name and Description Computation — the algorithm that decides what a screen reader actually says for a control. Establishes the precedence chain that trips up most custom components: aria-labelledby beats aria-label, and BOTH override the associated <label>, alt text, and visible button/link text, even when that visible text is correctly associated. The practical consequence: adding aria-label to a control that already has a visible label silently discards the visible label from the accessibility tree, breaking voice-control users who say what they see. Pairs with the APG page above for question part (6), and explains the mechanism behind SC 2.5.3 Label in Name.

results.title: The WebAIM Million — 2026 report on the accessibility of the top 1,000,000 home pages
results.snippet: The empirical backing for 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA', with fresh 2026 numbers. 82.7% of the million home pages now use ARIA (up from 79.4% in 2025), averaging 133+ ARIA attributes per page — over six times the 2019 figure. Pages WITH ARIA averaged 59.1 detected errors versus 42.0 for pages without; error count rises with ARIA count. WebAIM is careful that this is correlation not proven causation (ARIA-heavy pages are also more complex), which is the honest framing to cite. Overall: 56M+ distinct errors, 56.1 per page, a 10.1% year-over-year regression, against a 22.5% jump in average page element count. Useful as the hard evidence that the ARIA-first reflex is a net negative at population scale, and as the current state-of-the-web baseline for the legal-pressure sections of the question.

results.title: Accessibility Tips in Single-Page Applications — Deque
results.snippet: Covers question part (4): what breaks when a client-side route change replaces the page without a document load. SPAs void the browser contract that reset focus to the document root on navigation, so focus is stranded on the now-removed trigger element and the screen reader never announces the new view. Practitioner consensus documented here and echoed across the ecosystem (Dave Rupert, James Shakespeare, the react-router accessibility discussion): update document.title on every route change AND move focus deliberately — to the new view's <h1> or main container, with tabindex="-1" so it is programmatically focusable — optionally supplemented by a live-region announcement. Design-time implication: every route in the IA needs a designated focus target and a unique, meaningful title, which is an information-architecture decision made in the sitemap, not a code cleanup afterwards.

results.title: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2.2 to Mobile Applications (WCAG2Mobile) — W3C Group Draft Note
results.snippet: The single most important primary source for the native-vs-web divergence. W3C Group Draft Note published 6 May 2025 by the Mobile Accessibility Task Force (MATF), mapping every WCAG 2.2 Level A/AA criterion onto native iOS/Android, mobile web and hybrid apps. Its core move is terminology substitution: 'web page(s)' becomes 'screen(s)' or 'view(s)', 'set of web pages' becomes 'set of screens' — i.e. the unit of conformance shifts from the page to the screen, which is exactly the assumption WCAG bakes in and native breaks. Explicitly covers the 2.2 additions in a mobile frame (2.5.8 Target Size, 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.4 Motion Actuation, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry) and flags platform gaps such as 'not all mobile platforms provide a way to programmatically associate a label with non-text content'. Note the status caveat: informative, non-normative, and still a work in progress — several criteria sections are placeholders. MATF is also the group that drove orientation, reflow, pointer gestures, motion actuation, dragging, target size and redundant entry into WCAG 2.1/2.2 in the first place, which is why those criteria read as the most mobile-shaped ones.

results.title: Accessibility — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Apple's canonical design-time accessibility page, and the reference point for iOS's divergences from WCAG. Key design-time commitments: text must scale with Dynamic Type without truncating or overlapping (Apple asks for scaling to at least 200%, which is a layout decision made at wireframe stage, not a build-time fix), and every meaningful on-screen item needs a label or description a VoiceOver user perceives as speech or braille. Apple's minimum interactive target is 44x44 points — a different unit and a different number from both WCAG 2.5.8's 24 CSS px minimum / 2.5.5's 44 CSS px enhanced and Android's 48dp. The companion page developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover covers VoiceOver-specific design guidance. Pairs with the HIG index at developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines.

results.title: Principles for improving app accessibility — Android Developers
results.snippet: Android's primary design-time guidance and the direct counterpart to Apple's HIG page. Sets the 48dp x 48dp minimum focusable/touch-target area (larger is better), and makes the design point that a 24dp icon reaches the minimum via surrounding padding — the visual size and the target size are deliberately decoupled, which matters when a designer hands off a 24dp glyph. Requires that every interactive and meaningful element carry a label explaining its semantics — meaning and purpose, not appearance — with contentDescription mandatory on any element without visible text (ImageButton, ImageView). Note the three-way divergence in units and numbers across the platforms: 24 CSS px (WCAG 2.5.8 AA), 44pt (Apple), 48dp (Android). Companion pages: developer.android.com/guide/topics/ui/accessibility/apps and the Wear OS variant at /training/wearables/accessibility.

results.title: VoiceOver evaluation criteria — Accessibility Nutrition Labels, App Store Connect Help
results.snippet: A 2025-onward driver with no web equivalent: Apple's Accessibility Nutrition Labels are standardized App Store disclosures covering VoiceOver, Voice Control, Larger Text, Dark Interface, Differentiate Without Color Alone, Sufficient Contrast, Reduced Motion, Captions and Audio Descriptions. Unlike the EAA or DOJ Title II, this is platform-level rather than legal enforcement, but it forces the same decisions at concept time because the declaration is per-app and re-evaluated every update. The VoiceOver criteria are notably design-time: labels must be concise, make sense out of context, and must NOT include the control type ('New Message', not 'Press to compose a new message', and no 'checkbox' in the label) because the type comes from UIAccessibilityTraits instead — the trait system carries what ARIA role would carry on the web. Also demands that content reloads not reset VoiceOver cursor position and that screen changes move the cursor logically (the native analogue of SPA route-change focus management), that modals block background content, and that every complex gesture — drag/drop, multi-touch, long-press context menus — has an accessible alternative via custom actions. Related: WWDC25 session 224 'Evaluate your app for Accessibility Nutrition Labels'.

results.title: AccessibilityTraits — Apple Developer Documentation (SwiftUI)
results.snippet: The iOS trait system, which is where native semantics diverge most sharply from ARIA. Traits describe how an element behaves (isButton, isHeader, isStaticText, isSelected, allowsDirectInteraction, updatesFrequently) and are additive — accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader) — rather than a single exclusive role like ARIA's. Native controls come with traits already applied (Button gets isButton, Text gets isStaticText), which is the platform equivalent of the 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' rule: overriding a stock control's traits is usually the wrong answer. The adjustable trait plus accessibilityAdjustableAction is the iOS answer to a custom slider, replacing the web's aria-valuenow/valuemin/valuemax triple. UIKit's parallel is developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiaccessibilitytraits; the full modifier list is at developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view-accessibility.

results.title: Merging and clearing semantics — Jetpack Compose, Android Developers
results.snippet: Android's answer to accessible-name computation and grouping, and structurally unlike the web's. Compose maintains a semantics tree where Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) collapses child nodes into one announcement, with per-property merge strategies (ContentDescription concatenates descendant values into a list), while clearAndSetSemantics discards children entirely and substitutes an explicit description. There is no DOM and no aria-labelledby: the grouping decision — which composables form one TalkBack stop versus several — is made in the component tree at design/build time and is a genuine design decision, not a remediation. Related pages: /develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics (custom actions via the customActions property, the analogue of grouping row actions) and /develop/ui/compose/accessibility/api-defaults (what semantics stock components already supply, i.e. what you should not re-declare).

results.title: W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 — W3C Working Draft, 3 March 2026
results.snippet: The primary spec itself, latest draft 3 March 2026. Carries the explicit boilerplate: "This is a draft document and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any time. It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress." Defines the five per-section maturity labels designers need in order to read the draft correctly — Placeholder, Exploratory (direction-setting, details/definitions missing), Developing (roughly agreed, details in flux), Refining (ready for wide review and experimental adoption), Mature (ready for Recommendation). The Guidelines section is currently only at Developing; conformance is still Exploratory. Structure is Requirements (testable) + Assertions (documented statements about process, e.g. that usability testing with disabled users happened) + Methods (informative techniques). Load-bearing for the report's "what is stable" section: nothing in WCAG 3 has reached Refining, so nothing in it is safe to design against.

results.title: WCAG 3 Introduction | Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) | W3C
results.snippet: WAI's plain-language status page — the single best citation for "design against 2.2, not 3.0." States WCAG 3 "is currently an incomplete draft," that much of it "will change substantially," and that it "is not expected to be a completed W3C standard for a few more years." Critically for procurement and roadmap planning: "WCAG 3 will not supersede WCAG 2 and WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for at least several years after WCAG 3 is finalized" — so WCAG 2.2 AA remains the design target well into the 2030s. Also documents the March 2026 terminology churn that trips up anyone reading older commentary: "Foundational Requirements" became "Core Requirements," and what earlier drafts called "Outcomes" are now "Requirements," with Guidelines carrying the plain-language outcome statement. Notes AGWG planned to publish a projected WCAG 3 timeline by April 2026.

results.title: Explainer for W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 — W3C Draft Note, 3 March 2026
results.snippet: The companion explainer, same 3 March 2026 date, and the clearest primary description of the proposed conformance model. Bronze/Silver/Gold replaces A/AA/AAA: every level requires all Core Requirements; higher levels add a proportion of Supplemental Requirements plus Assertions. Assertions are the genuinely new design-time concept — "an attributable and documented statement of fact regarding procedures practiced in the development and maintenance of the content," i.e. process claims a tester cannot independently verify, which pushes accessibility work upstream into concept and design where the report's thesis lives. Also candid about instability: AGWG is still "exploring whether meeting the higher levels would work best based on points, percentages, or predefined sets of provisions (modules)," the conformance section is Exploratory, and "developing and vetting the conformance model is a large portion of the work AGWG needs to complete over the next few years." Confirms WCAG 3 "does not deprecate WCAG 2."

results.title: For Review: WCAG 3 Working Draft – March 2026 | W3C WAI News
results.snippet: The dated publication announcement establishing that the most recent WCAG 3 draft is 3 March 2026 (the prior one was 4 September 2025) — useful as the citable "as of" anchor so the report does not appear to be reading a stale draft. Framed purely as a call for comment (via wai@w3.org or GitHub), with no timeline commitment and no readiness claim, which is itself the finding: W3C is still soliciting direction-level feedback rather than stabilising text. Points readers to the WCAG 3 Introduction and the in-progress-drafts status page for maturity levels.

results.title: WCAG 2.2 Approved as an ISO Standard | W3C WAI News (21 October 2025)
results.snippet: The counterweight to the WCAG 3 churn and the strongest evidence for what IS stable. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation (12 December 2024 edition) and was subsequently approved as an ISO/IEC standard in October 2025 — ISO ratification is a hardening event, not a stepping stone, and it is what national procurement rules and regulators reference. Supports the report's practical instruction: design to WCAG 2.2 AA, including the six new SCs (2.4.11/2.4.12 focus not obscured, 2.5.7 dragging movements, 2.5.8 target size minimum, 3.2.6 consistent help, 3.3.7 redundant entry, 3.3.8 accessible authentication), and treat WCAG 3 as a watch item. Note the companion fact from the spec: SC 4.1.1 Parsing was removed in 2.2 but may still need reporting under policies pinned to 2.0/2.1.

results.title: Draft EN 301 549 V4.1.0 (2025-11) — Harmonised European Standard, ETSI (primary PDF)
results.snippet: The actual near-term roadmap item with legal teeth, as opposed to WCAG 3's speculative one. The harmonised standard currently cited in the EU Official Journal is EN 301 549 v3.2.1 (2021), which incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA — so the European Accessibility Act, applicable since 28 June 2025, presumes conformance against 2.1 AA today. Draft v4.1.0 went to public review November 2025 and the final v4.1.x, which incorporates WCAG 2.2 AA, is expected to be cited in the OJEU during 2026. Design implication worth stating explicitly in the report: the WCAG 2.2-only criteria (target size, dragging, focus not obscured, consistent help, redundant entry, accessible authentication) are not yet formally binding in the EU harmonised route but become so on that citation, which is 2026 — a far more actionable deadline than anything in WCAG 3.

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 adds exactly nine new success criteria over WCAG 2.1: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum, AA), 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced, AAA), 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA), 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum, AA), 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A), 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A), 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum, AA), 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced, AAA). Six of the nine are at level A or AA and therefore in scope for the AA conformance target used by EN 301 549 and Section 508.
claims.quote: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA); 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) (AAA); 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA); 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA); 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA); 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A); 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A); 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA); 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (AAA)

claims.claim: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) sets a concrete numeric threshold designers can spec at layout time: interactive targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or else have sufficient spacing around them — making it a design-system token decision (hit area, tap spacing) rather than a post-build audit item.
claims.quote: Ensure targets meet a minimum size or have sufficient spacing around them. … at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels

claims.claim: 2.5.7 Dragging Movements requires that any drag-based interaction also have a single-pointer alternative, which forces an interaction-design decision (e.g. a reorder menu or move buttons alongside drag-and-drop) at concept time rather than a code fix later.
claims.quote: For any action that involves dragging, provide a simple pointer alternative.

claims.claim: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum, AA) requires focused elements to be at least partially visible, and 2.4.12 (AAA) requires them to be fully visible — a constraint on sticky headers, cookie banners, and floating toolbars, i.e. a layout/chrome decision. 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA) further specifies a focus indicator at least as large as a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter with a contrast ratio of at least 3:1.
claims.quote: Ensure when an item gets keyboard focus, it is at least partially visible. … Ensure when an item gets keyboard focus, it is fully visible. … at least as large as the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter … a contrast ratio of at least 3:1.

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023, and the 2.0 and 2.1 success criteria carry over essentially unchanged with one exception: 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed in 2.2. So conformance to 2.2 subsumes 2.1 except for that removed criterion.
claims.quote: WCAG 2.2 was published as a 'W3C Recommendation' web standard on 5 October 2023. … The 2.0 and 2.1 success criteria are essentially the same in 2.2, with one exception … 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed from WCAG 2.2.

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) is a Level AA criterion requiring pointer targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, measured by whether a solid 24x24 CSS pixel axis-aligned square fits entirely within the target — a hit-area dimension a designer must specify at layout time, not patch after build.
claims.quote: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels ... For a target to be 'at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels', it must be conceptually possible to draw a solid 24 by 24 CSS pixel square, aligned to the horizontal and vertical axis such that the square is completely within the target.

claims.claim: Undersized targets can still conform via the Spacing exception, evaluated by centering a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle on each undersized target's bounding box and confirming the circles do not intersect another target — making inter-target spacing (not just component size) a design-time decision.
claims.quote: Undersized targets are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target.

claims.claim: SC 2.5.8 has exactly five exceptions — Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, and Essential — including an Equivalent exception that is satisfied if the same function is reachable through a different conforming control on the same page, which is an information-architecture decision made at concept time.
claims.quote: The function can be achieved through a different control on the same page that meets this criterion.

claims.claim: Inline links inside sentences are out of scope for 2.5.8 when their size is constrained by the line-height of surrounding non-target text, because enforcing the 24px rule on text-embedded links produces poor design outcomes.
claims.quote: The success criterion does not apply to inline targets in sentences, or where the size of the target is constrained by the line-height of non-target text. ... Applying this success criterion when multiple links are embedded in blocks of smaller text often results in an undesirable design.

claims.claim: W3C's stated best practice exceeds the pass threshold: authors should meet the 24x24 minimum size regardless of whether the spacing exception would let them pass, and should consider the Level AAA 44 CSS pixel target (SC 2.5.5) for important controls.
claims.quote: As a best practice it is recommended to at least meet the minimum size requirement of the Success Criterion, regardless of spacing. ... For important links/controls, consider aiming for the stricter 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced).

result.publishDate: Last updated May 11, 2026 (W3C WCAG 2.2 Understanding document; SC 2.5.8 introduced in WCAG 2.2, W3C Recommendation October 2023)

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) is a Level AA requirement that forbids any cognitive function test in any step of an authentication process unless that step offers one of exactly four exceptions: Alternative, Mechanism, Object Recognition, or Personal Content.
claims.quote: A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of the following: Alternative, Mechanism, Object Recognition, Personal Content.

claims.claim: The prohibited 'cognitive function tests' are enumerated concretely and include memorization (username, password, characters, images, or patterns), transcription (typing in characters), performing calculations, and solving puzzles — which means a design that asks a user to read a one-time code on one device and retype it on another is a failing pattern absent an exception.
claims.quote: memorization, such as remembering a username, password, set of characters, images, or patterns

claims.claim: Supporting password managers and permitting copy-paste into username and password fields is an accepted way to satisfy the 'Mechanism' exception; conversely, blocking paste or preventing re-entry of a password/code in the same format is a failure of the criterion.
claims.quote: Users can copy their login credentials from a local source (such as a standalone third-party password manager) and paste it into the username and password fields.

claims.claim: Object-recognition CAPTCHAs are explicitly permitted at Level AA under 3.3.8 but are not excepted at Level AAA under SC 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced), so the choice of CAPTCHA type is a conformance-level-dependent design decision.
claims.quote: are not excepted in Success Criterion 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) at AAA level

claims.claim: The 'Personal Content' exception is limited to identifying non-text content that the user themselves supplied to the site, not arbitrary knowledge-based questions.
claims.quote: The cognitive function test is to identify non-text content the user provided to the website.

result.publishDate: 2026-05-11 (page \"Updated\" date; WCAG 2.2 itself became a W3C Recommendation 5 October 2023)

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) is Level AA and sets a hard numeric floor of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for pointer targets, with named exceptions (spacing, equivalent target elsewhere, inline targets, user-agent control, essential) — making minimum hit-area a component-spec decision, not a post-build audit fix.
claims.quote: The target for pointer input is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels in size, except where: [Spacing] Inline targets and targets in user interface components where the associated label is part of the click target; [Equivalent] Functionality available through equivalent targets at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels; [User agent control]

claims.claim: SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (Level AA) requires that any drag-operated functionality also be operable by a single pointer action without dragging unless dragging is essential — so every drag interaction (reorder lists, sliders, kanban, map pan, drag-to-upload) must be designed with a non-drag equivalent from the concept stage.
claims.quote: Functionality that can be operated by dragging movements can also be operated by single pointer actions without dragging, unless dragging is essential.

claims.claim: SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), Level AA, forbids requiring a cognitive function test (memorization, transcription, puzzle-solving) in any authentication step unless essential, with only object-recognition and personal-content exceptions — this rules out designs that mandate password memorization without paste/password-manager support, or traditional text CAPTCHAs, as the sole login path.
claims.quote: A mechanism is available that does not rely on cognitive function test to authenticate, except where that test is essential. [Object recognition] Identifying objects; [Personal content] User-provided information

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 splits focus obscuring into two levels with different thresholds: 2.4.11 (Level AA) only forbids the focused component being *entirely* hidden by author content, while 2.4.12 (Level AAA) forbids *any part* being hidden — meaning sticky headers/footers, cookie banners and floating chat widgets must be sized and positioned against these thresholds at layout time.
claims.quote: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) - Level AA: "When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content." 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) - Level AAA: "When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, no part of the component is hidden by author-created content."

claims.claim: SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry is Level A (the lowest conformance tier, not AA), requiring previously entered information to be available for re-use except where re-entry is essential or the information is security-sensitive — pushing multi-step flow and checkout design decisions to auto-populate or offer prior values.
claims.quote: Information previously entered by or provided to the user is available for re-use, except where re-entering is essential or information is sensitive for security purposes.

result.publishDate: 2024-12-12 (W3C Recommendation; document status line reads \"W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024\" — this is the updated Recommendation; WCAG 2.2 was originally published as a Recommendation 5 October 2023)

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 adds nine success criteria over WCAG 2.1, all of which are indexed on the official W3C Understanding page: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced), 2.4.13 Focus Appearance, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), and 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced).
claims.quote: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) … 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) … 2.4.13 Focus Appearance … 2.5.7 Dragging Movements … 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) … 3.2.6 Consistent Help … 3.3.7 Redundant Entry … 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) … 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)

claims.claim: SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) is Level AA and sets a hard numeric design threshold of 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with exactly five escape hatches — spacing (a 24px-diameter circle centered on each undersized target must not intersect another target), equivalent control, inline text, user-agent control, and essential/legally-required presentation. This is a measurable value a designer must set in the comp, not something a build check can retrofit.
claims.quote: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when: … Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target

claims.claim: SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), Level AA, prohibits any cognitive function test in an authentication step, and W3C explicitly defines that test to include remembering a password, transcribing characters, correct spelling, calculations, and solving puzzles — meaning conventional password-plus-CAPTCHA login flows fail unless one of four exceptions applies (alternative method, assistive mechanism, object recognition, or user-provided personal content).
claims.quote: A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of the following … memorization, such as remembering a username, password, set of characters, images, or patterns; transcription, such as typing in characters; use of correct spelling; performance of calculations; solving of puzzles.

claims.claim: Actively blocking password managers, autofill, or copy-and-paste in login fields is a stated failure of SC 3.3.8 — so a common security-team design decision (disable paste on password fields) is itself the accessibility defect, and must be settled at design time.
claims.quote: If user agents and password managers are actively blocked from filling in the fields (for instance, by a script that prevents form fields from being automatically populated), or users are prevented from copy and paste operations...then the page would fail this criterion unless an alternative is provided.

claims.claim: The Understanding documents are informative supporting material, not part of the normative WCAG standard — so their techniques and thresholds beyond the criterion text cannot be cited as binding conformance requirements; only the success criteria themselves are normative. The index also records that SC 4.1.1 Parsing has been made obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2.
claims.quote: informative, not part of the 'normative' WCAG standard … 4.1.1 Parsing (Obsolete and removed)

results.title: DOJ Interim Final Rule: Extension of Compliance Dates for ADA Title II Web Accessibility (28 CFR Part 35), Fed. Reg. 2026-07663
results.snippet: The single most important legal update since the original brief was framed: on 20 April 2026 DOJ published an interim final rule pushing the Title II web/mobile deadlines back one year. The April 24, 2026 date for entities serving populations of 50,000+ is now April 26, 2027, and small entities/special districts move from April 26, 2027 to April 26, 2028. Substance is unchanged — WCAG 2.1 Level AA (A + AA success criteria and conformance requirements) for web content AND mobile apps. Any answer citing 'April 2026' as a live deadline is now wrong. Note the ceiling: this defers the regulatory deadline, not ADA liability — Title II effective-communication obligations and private litigation continue regardless.

results.title: Fact Sheet: New Rule on the Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps Provided by State and Local Governments — ADA.gov
results.snippet: DOJ's own plain-language statement of the rule, updated to reflect the 2026 extension (2027/2028 tiers). Directly useful for the design-time framing because it enumerates the five exceptions that are themselves *design and content-strategy decisions*, not post-build checks: archived content, pre-existing electronic documents (PDF/Word/spreadsheets posted before the compliance date), third-party user-generated content, password-protected individualized documents, and pre-compliance social media posts. Whether something lands inside an exception depends on how the information architecture and document pipeline were designed. Also confirms mobile apps are in scope on identical terms to web — the bridge to the native iOS/Android part of the question.

results.title: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) — official consolidated text, EUR-Lex
results.snippet: The authoritative EAA text (OJ L 151, 7.6.2019, pp. 70–115). Applicable since 28 June 2025 across all 27 Member States. Critical design-time detail the secondary coverage usually omits: the EAA is a directive, so obligations and penalties are set by 27 separate national transpositions (Germany's BFSG, France's, Sweden's, etc.), each with its own enforcement authority and fine ceiling — there is no single EU-wide penalty. Also carries the transition rule that matters for legacy work: service contracts concluded before 28 June 2025 may continue until 28 June 2030, and self-service terminals stay usable for their economic life up to 20 years. The Annex I functional requirements are written as outcome requirements (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust) for products AND services, which is why they bind concept-stage decisions rather than a code audit.

results.title: ETSI EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (2021-03) — Harmonised European Standard: Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services (official PDF)
results.snippet: The actual technical standard behind the EAA and EU public-sector Directive 2016/2102 — free official download, no paywall. V3.2.1 incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA in full, so the currently-cited European standard does NOT yet include the WCAG 2.2 criteria (2.5.7, 2.5.8, 2.4.11, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8) the question focuses on. Successor V4.1.1, which adds WCAG 2.2 plus expanded Real-Time Text requirements, was drafted as V4.1.0 in Nov 2025 and is expected to be cited in the Official Journal around October 2026 — i.e. WCAG 2.2 is a near-term legal obligation in the EU, not just best practice. EN 301 549 also reaches well beyond WCAG: clause 5 generic requirements, clause 8 hardware, clause 11 non-web software (which is what governs native iOS/Android apps), clause 12 documentation and support services, and clause 6 two-way voice/RTT.

results.title: The EAA and BFSG: Recap and Update — What has happened in the first year since June 28, 2025 (Taylor Wessing, June 2026)
results.snippet: Answers the 'what has enforcement actually looked like' half of the angle, which no primary source can. One year in: no confirmed monetary fine has been issued under any national EAA transposition. What has happened instead is formal notices (France, to major retailers, July 2025), the Swedish PTS opening its first e-commerce accessibility cases (Oct 2025), German law firms sending private Abmahnung warning letters to e-commerce operators within weeks of the BFSG taking effect, and civil-society litigation in French Commercial Court (Nov 2025; the Auchan case was heard May 2026 and dismissed on procedural grounds, though the court accepted the site was inaccessible). Useful calibration for the brief: the near-term EAA risk is notice-and-remediation and private warning letters, not headline fines — which makes design-time decisions a cost-avoidance argument rather than a fine-avoidance one.

results.title: IT Accessibility Laws and Policies — Section508.gov (reviewed/updated July 2026)
results.snippet: Confirms the point most 2026 write-ups get wrong: Section 508 is still frozen at the Access Board's January 2017 refresh (effective January 18, 2018), which incorporates WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA by reference — not 2.1, not 2.2. As of a July 2026 review there is no pending Access Board rulemaking to update it. That produces the practical split a designer has to hold in mind: federal ICT procurement (508) = WCAG 2.0 AA, state/local government web and apps (Title II) = WCAG 2.1 AA by 2027/2028, EU = WCAG 2.1 AA now and 2.2 once EN 301 549 V4.1.1 is cited. Design to WCAG 2.2 and every regime is satisfied; design to the floor of any one and you fail the others.

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) is a Level AA criterion whose normative requirement is that a keyboard-focused component must not be ENTIRELY hidden by author-created content — partial obscuring passes at AA, while the AAA sibling 2.4.12 (Enhanced) requires no part of the focused component be obscured.
claims.quote: When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content.

claims.claim: The criterion targets specific, common design-time layout decisions: sticky headers, sticky footers, and non-modal dialogs are named as the typical content types that overlap focused items — meaning the decision to use a persistent overlay is itself the accessibility decision.
claims.quote: Typical types of content that can overlap focused items are sticky footers, sticky headers, and non-modal dialogs.

claims.claim: For cookie banners and similar overlays, W3C names two concrete passing designs decided at design time: make the banner modal so it must be dismissed before page navigation, or apply CSS scroll padding so the banner never overlaps other content.
claims.quote: Ways of passing include making the banner modal so the user has to dismiss the banner before navigating through the page, or using scroll padding so the banner does not overlap other content.

claims.claim: In user-configurable/repositionable interfaces (e.g. movable panels or widgets), only the INITIAL position of user-movable content is in scope for testing and conformance — the author is not responsible for obscuring the user themselves causes by moving content.
claims.quote: Where content in a configurable interface can be repositioned by the user, then only the initial positions of user-movable content are considered for testing and conformance of this success criterion.

claims.claim: Content the user themselves opened does not violate 2.4.11 if the focused component can be revealed without advancing keyboard focus — i.e. the escape route must not require navigating back to the opened content to dismiss it.
claims.quote: Content opened by the user may obscure the component receiving focus. If the user can reveal the focused component without advancing the keyboard focus, the component with focus is not considered visually hidden due to author-created content.

claims.claim: The APG defines an ARIA role as a binding promise: because ARIA roles do not cause browsers to supply keyboard behaviors or styling (unlike native HTML input elements), applying role="button" to a div obligates the author to implement the button's expected keyboard interactions in JavaScript. This makes role assignment a design-time commitment to a full interaction model, not a labeling step.
claims.quote: Is a promise that the author of that <div> has also incorporated JavaScript that provides the keyboard interactions expected for a button. Unlike HTML input elements, ARIA roles do not cause browsers to provide keyboard behaviors or styling. Using a role without fulfilling the promise of that role is similar to making a "Place Order" button that abandons an order and empties the shopping cart.

claims.claim: ARIA can cloak (override) native semantics, and the APG names concrete cases where applying ARIA destroys accessibility rather than adding it: role="menuitem" on an anchor makes AT users perceive a menu item instead of a link; aria-label on a link makes the link text unperceivable to AT users; role="log" on a table removes table semantics; and role="navigation" on a <ul> is flagged as an outright ERROR because its <li> children are no longer inside a list.
claims.quote:
Some of ARIA is like a cloak; it covers up, or overrides, the original semantics or content. …
  • nav link 1
  • nav link 2

claims.claim: The APG's code deliberately contains no workarounds for gaps in browser and assistive-technology support for ARIA 1.2, so copying APG patterns into production without testing each relevant browser + AT combination is explicitly unsafe; the guide states testing interoperability is essential before production use.
claims.quote: Testing assistive technology interoperability is essential before using code from this guide in production. Because the purpose of this guide is to illustrate appropriate use of ARIA 1.2 as defined in the ARIA specification, the design patterns, reference examples, and sample code intentionally do not describe and implement coding techniques for working around problems caused by gaps in support for ARIA 1.2 in browsers and assistive technologies.

claims.claim: The APG provides no mobile or touch compatibility information for its examples; some ARIA features are supported in no mobile browser at all, and no standardized approach exists for touch interactions that work across mobile browsers — meaning APG patterns cannot be assumed to transfer to touch/mobile contexts.
claims.quote: Currently, this guide does not indicate which examples are compatible with mobile browsers or touch interfaces. While some of the examples include specific features that enhance mobile and touch support, some ARIA features are not supported in any mobile browser. In addition, there is not yet a standardized approach for providing touch interactions that work across mobile browsers.

claims.claim: The APG's stated rationale for "No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA" is that ARIA functions as a presentation layer for assistive technologies — analogous to CSS — and therefore incorrect ARIA misrepresents the visual experience to non-visual users rather than merely failing to help.
claims.quote: Functionally, ARIA roles, states, and properties are analogous to a CSS for assistive technologies. For screen reader users, ARIA controls the rendering of their non-visual experience. Incorrect ARIA misrepresents visual experiences, with potentially devastating effects on their corresponding non-visual experiences.

result.publishDate: No publication or last-updated date is shown on the page; footer reads "Copyright © 2026 World Wide Web Consortium". Content targets ARIA 1.2.

claims.claim: aria-labelledby sits at the top of the accessible name computation hierarchy and overrides every other naming source, including aria-label, the <label> element for form controls, alt text on images, button values, and link text — so a designer/developer adding ARIA can silently destroy a correct visible label.
claims.quote: ARIA labels are always at the top of the accessible name hierarchy. `aria-labelledby` will override any other information that could serve as an accessible name, including `aria-label`, `<label>` for form controls, the `alt` attribute for images, button values for buttons, and link text for links.

claims.claim: When aria-label overrides a visible <label>, speech-input users cannot activate the control by speaking the visible text — a concrete case where adding ARIA makes the interface less accessible than no ARIA at all.
claims.quote: a screen reader would be presented with 'Your Name' when they navigate into the field, and nothing will happen if a Dragon user says 'Click First Name.'

claims.claim: WCAG SC 2.5.3 Label in Name requires that the accessible name of a link or control contain the visible text label, but does not require an exact match — e.g. an accessible name of "Next Page" satisfies a visible label of "Next".
claims.quote: Label in Name requires that the accessible _name_ for a link or control contain the text _label_.

claims.claim: A mismatch between visible label and accessible name is a voice-control failure mode specifically, not only a screen reader issue: voice control users address controls by their visible text.
claims.quote: A user of voice control software like Dragon would be unable to activate this link using the visible label.

claims.claim: The placeholder attribute must not be substituted for a real label, and the title attribute is only picked up as the accessible name when no associated <label> element exists — making the native <label> the correct design-time decision over placeholder/title patterns.
claims.quote: The placeholder attribute should not be used as an alternative to a label

claims.claim: Screen readers do not reliably honor the polite/assertive distinction: in Adrian Roselli's testing, JAWS 2026 with Chrome 143/144 treated all live regions as polite, and NVDA (2024.1/2025.3.2) with Firefox treated polite, assertive, and <output> regions alike as polite — announcing at the first break rather than at the end of a sentence.
claims.quote: All live regions treated as polite (announces at first break, which is not at end of sentence).

claims.claim: role="alert" does not produce the expected "alert" prefix in announcements across JAWS, Narrator, VoiceOver, and TalkBack, so designers cannot rely on the role itself to convey urgency to screen reader users — the urgency must be carried by the message text.
claims.quote: `alert` role does not pre-pend announcement with alert.

claims.claim: A live region that is hidden — via the hidden attribute, aria-hidden, or display:none — does not announce in any tested screen reader/browser combination, so the common pattern of populating a hidden region and then revealing it, or keeping the region hidden, fails universally.
claims.quote: No live region announces when hidden

claims.claim: The HTML <output> element is not a reliable substitute for an explicit aria-live region: its support is inconsistent across the tested matrix, with Narrator failing to announce it in some versions.
claims.quote: Polite, assertive, and `<output>` live regions treated as polite (announces at first break, which is not at end of sentence).

claims.claim: The findings come from a hands-on support matrix Roselli has maintained since mid-2024, tested across NVDA, JAWS, Narrator, VoiceOver (macOS and iOS), Orca, and TalkBack on Firefox, Chrome, Edge, and Safari across Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS — meaning the failure modes are documented behavior, not speculation, and the article documents how live regions behave rather than prescribing whether to use them.
claims.quote: I made this demo in mid-2024 to demonstrate a problem.

claims.claim: The accessible name calculation follows a fixed precedence order that authors cannot override: aria-labelledby is used first, then aria-label, then host-language attributes (HTML label, legend, caption, alt), then content from child elements for roles that support it, and only last the fallback attributes title and placeholder.
claims.quote: The `aria-labelledby` property is used if present. ... If the name is still empty, the `aria-label` property is used if present.

claims.claim: Applying aria-label or aria-labelledby to an element whose role supports naming from child content hides that element's contents and all its descendants from assistive technology users — a concrete case where adding ARIA actively breaks the interface rather than improving it.
claims.quote: If an element with one of the above roles that supports naming from child content is named by using `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, content contained in the element and its descendants is hidden from assistive technology users.

claims.claim: Both the WAI-ARIA specification and WCAG require every focusable, interactive element to have an accessible name — making 'does this control have a visible, nameable label?' a design-time requirement, not a build-time check; and certain element types (paragraphs, list items) must not be named with aria-label at all.
claims.quote: Both the WAI-ARIA specification and WCAG require all focusable, interactive elements to have an accessible name. ... There are certain types of elements, such as paragraphs and list items, that should not be named with `aria-label`.

claims.claim: APG's cardinal rules direct authors to prefer visible text and native HTML naming techniques (the label element for form controls, caption for tables) over ARIA attributes, because visible text simplifies maintenance, prevents bugs, and reduces translation requirements.
claims.quote: In HTML documents, whenever possible, rely on HTML naming techniques, such as the HTML `label` element for form elements and `caption` element for tables.

claims.claim: The title and placeholder attributes are explicitly characterized as low-quality, ineffective naming methods because naming is not their purpose; effective names should instead be concise (one to three words for many elements) and lead with the most distinguishing words.
claims.quote: Because the purpose of these attributes is not naming, their content typically yields low quality accessible names that are not effective.

result.publishDate: Not stated on page (W3C WAI ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, continuously maintained; no publication or last-updated date surfaced in the fetched content)

claims.claim: Deque prescribes three interchangeable-or-combined mechanisms for making client-side view (route) changes perceivable to screen reader users: updating the page title, ARIA live regions, and/or moving focus — i.e. an SPA that silently swaps the view without one of these is a defect.
claims.quote: Make sure that client-side view changes are known to screen reader users by announcing the change in page title, using ARIA live regions and/or focus management.

claims.claim: Accessibility cost rises the later it is addressed, and the correct starting point is UX and Design rather than the build or audit phase.
claims.quote: It's easier and less costly to incorporate accessibility the earlier you tackle it, starting with UX and Design.

claims.claim: Custom/complex interaction patterns should be prototyped early with accessibility included, and designers/developers should consult the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices for already-solved interaction patterns rather than inventing new ones.
claims.quote: Prototype complex or custom interactions early, and include accessibility. ... Check out the ARIA Authoring Practices for known interaction patterns.

claims.claim: Making every element focusable is a design error: screen readers provide navigation modes other than the TAB key, so tab-stop count is not a proxy for screen reader accessibility.
claims.quote: Screen readers have ways of navigating other than using the TAB key, so you don't need to make everything focusable.

claims.claim: Focus management in JavaScript is treated as a testable engineering requirement, not a manual QA nicety — it should be covered by automated tests.
claims.quote: Get comfortable with focus management in JavaScript, and write it into your automated tests.

claims.claim: In the 2026 WebAIM Million analysis of the top 1,000,000 home pages, 95.9% had automatically detectable WCAG 2 conformance failures — up from 94.8% in 2025 — with 56,114,377 distinct errors detected, an average of 56.1 errors per page (up 10.1% from 51 in 2025).
claims.quote: 95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures. ... Across the one million home pages, 56,114,377 distinct accessibility errors were detected—an average of 56.1 errors per page.

claims.claim: Low contrast text below WCAG 2 AA thresholds is the single most prevalent detectable failure, found on 83.9% of home pages in 2026 (up from 79.1% in 2025) — a failure class fixed entirely by color/typography choices made at design time, not by code.
claims.quote: Low contrast text, below the WCAG 2 AA thresholds, was found on 83.9% of home pages

claims.claim: ARIA usage is growing fast (133,589,803 attributes detected, over 133 per page on average, +27% in one year and over 6x the 2019 level), yet home pages with ARIA present averaged 59.1 errors versus 42 errors on pages without ARIA — empirical support for the 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' rule.
claims.quote: 133,589,803 ARIA attributes were detected—over 133 per page on average! ARIA code increased 27% in just one year and is over 6 times higher than it was in 2019. ... Home pages with ARIA present had significantly more errors (59.1 on average) than pages without ARIA (42 on average)

claims.claim: Missing accessible names remain endemic in real-world pages: one third (33.1%) of form inputs were not properly labeled, missing form input labels appeared on 51% of home pages, empty links on 46.3%, and empty buttons on 30.6%.
claims.quote: One third (33.1%) of those form inputs were not properly labeled

claims.claim: Six error categories — low contrast text, missing image alt text, missing form input labels, empty links, empty buttons, and missing document language — account for 96% of all detected errors, meaning nearly all machine-detectable accessibility failure is concentrated in a small, largely design-time-decidable set. Missing alt text specifically affected 16.2% of all home page images (10.8 per page).
claims.quote: 96% of all errors detected fall into these six categories.

claims.claim: W3C's mobile guidance says WCAG alone is not a sufficient accessibility standard for mobile applications — conforming to WCAG 2.2 does not cover all accessibility requirements of a native app, so mobile teams need platform guidance on top of it.
claims.quote: This document is not sufficient by itself to ensure accessibility in mobile applications — as a web standard, WCAG does not fully cover all accessibility requirements

claims.claim: For mobile applications, WCAG 2.2's web-specific terms are reinterpreted: 'web page(s)' becomes 'screen(s)'/'view(s)', and the unit of evaluation for 'set of web pages' is a 'set of screens' — explicitly departing from WCAG2ICT's earlier interpretation of 'set of software'. This changes the scope over which criteria like Consistent Help (3.2.6) and Consistent Navigation are judged in an app.
claims.quote: When certain Web-specific terms or phrases like 'web page(s)' were used in success criteria, those were replaced with mobile terms or phrases like 'screen(s)' or 'view(s)' … the equivalent unit of evaluation for a 'set of web pages' would be a 'set of screens', not — as previously interpreted in WCAG2ICT — as a 'set of software'

claims.claim: WCAG2Mobile is non-normative: it is a W3C Group Draft Note, not a standard, and does not define conformance for mobile apps — so it cannot be cited as a compliance target the way WCAG 2.2 or EN 301 549 can.
claims.quote: This document is purely an informative note about mobile applications, not a standard, so it does not describe how mobile applications should conform to it.

claims.claim: In native software, 'programmatically determinable' (the basis for accessible names, roles, and states) is satisfied through the platform's accessibility services/APIs rather than web markup or ARIA — the native equivalent of the web's accessibility tree contract.
claims.quote: In software, programmatic determinability is best achieved through the use of accessibility services provided by platform software to enable interoperability between software and assistive technologies and accessibility features of software.

claims.claim: WCAG's 'keyboard interface' requirement applies to touch-only mobile devices with no physical keyboard, because the term denotes the software interface to any keyboard or keyboard substitute, not a hardware keyboard.
claims.quote: Keyboard interface does not refer to a physical device but to the interface between the software and any keyboard or keyboard substitute.

claims.claim: WCAG 3.0 remains a W3C Working Draft as of 3 March 2026 and the Working Group itself states the specification still has several years of work remaining — so no 2026 design or procurement decision can be anchored to WCAG 3 conformance.
claims.quote: This draft includes an updated list of the potential guidelines, requirements, and assertions that have progressed to Developing status. While this draft has moved closer towards completion, it still has several years of work.

claims.claim: WCAG 3 will not replace WCAG 2; the W3C explicitly states WCAG 2 will continue to be the legally required standard in many countries for a long time, meaning WCAG 2.2 is the operative design-time target.
claims.quote: WCAG 3 does not replace WCAG 2. WCAG 2 is used around the world and will still be required by different countries for a long time to come.

claims.claim: WCAG 2.2 Level A + AA conformance is expected to satisfy most, but not all, of WCAG 3's minimum conformance level; WCAG 3 adds tests and uses different scoring mechanics, so a 2.2-conformant product will still require additional work later.
claims.quote: Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 Level A and Level AA is expected to meet most of the minimum conformance level of this new standard but, since WCAG 3 includes additional tests and different scoring mechanics, additional work will be needed to reach full conformance.

claims.claim: WCAG 3.0 tracks each section through five maturity stages (Placeholder, Exploratory, Developing, Refining, Mature), and the March 2026 draft contains only content that has reached 'Developing' — the stage where scope is roughly agreed but details are incomplete, two stages short of 'Mature'.
claims.quote: This is an update to W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0. It includes all requirements that have reached the developing status.

claims.claim: The W3C forbids citing the WCAG 3.0 draft as anything other than work in progress, which rules out its use as a basis for policy, contracts, or compliance claims.
claims.quote: This is a draft document and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any time. It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress.

claims.claim: Gesture-only interactions on Android (swipe to dismiss, drag to reorder) are inaccessible unless the developer explicitly declares an equivalent CustomAccessibilityAction with a label — the Android analogue of WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, and a decision that must be made when the gesture is designed, not patched afterward.
claims.quote: By adding accessibility actions, you can enable users of accessibility services to complete critical user flows within your app.

claims.claim: Android divides responsibility the same way the 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' rule does for the web: standard Material/Compose/Foundation components (Button, Switch, Checkbox) ship with correct role and stateDescription semantics by default, and only custom components drawn with lower-level APIs require the developer to author semantics manually — including role, stateDescription and action labels.
claims.quote: If you need highly custom UI elements not covered by standard composables, you can build them using lower-level drawing APIs (like `androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Canvas`) or `Layout` composables. In such cases, you must explicitly define their accessibility properties using `Modifier.semantics`.

claims.claim: Android's equivalent of announcing a view/route change is the pane title, available from Android 9 (API 28), and TalkBack treats pane titles as identifiers — so reusing generic titles such as 'List' or 'Details' across independent screens produces unpredictable accessibility behavior. This makes screen/pane naming a design-time information-architecture decision, not an implementation detail.
claims.quote: Use unique pane titles across your app. Because TalkBack uses pane titles as identifiers, reusing generic titles (like "List" or "Details") on completely independent screens can cause unintended side effects and unpredictable accessibility behavior.

claims.claim: Grouping of related content for screen readers is a layout decision: elements that form a natural group must be placed in a parent container with mergeDescendants set to true, and interactivity must live only on that parent — adding clickable or focusable to inner children breaks the grouping.
claims.quote: When grouping related elements like in the previous example, make only the parent container interactive. Avoid adding `clickable` or `focusable` modifiers to the inner child elements.

claims.claim: Android's official principles page states the non-color-cue requirement (the platform counterpart of WCAG 1.4.1) but specifies no numeric thresholds at all — it names no minimum touch target size in dp, no contrast ratio, and no minimum font size, unlike WCAG 2.2's quantified criteria such as 2.5.8 target size 24x24 CSS pixels.
claims.quote: To assist users with color vision deficiencies, use cues other than color to distinguish UI elements within your app's screens. These techniques can include using different shapes or sizes, providing text or visual patterns, or adding audio- or touch-based (haptic) feedback to mark the elements' differences.

claims.claim: WCAG 3 is not a finished W3C standard and W3C does not expect it to become one for several more years; as of this page the working group had not yet even published a projected timeline, planning to produce one by April 2026.
claims.quote: WCAG 3 is not expected to be a completed W3C standard for a few more years. ... plans to develop a projected WCAG 3 timeline by April 2026.

claims.claim: WCAG 2.x remains the operative normative target for the foreseeable future: WCAG 3 will not supersede WCAG 2, and WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for at least several years after WCAG 3 is finalized.
claims.quote: WCAG 3 will not supersede WCAG 2 and WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for at least several years after WCAG 3 is finalized.

claims.claim: The current WCAG 3 draft cannot be used as a design or compliance target, because its content is explicitly exploratory and W3C states the final requirements will differ from the draft.
claims.quote: Many aspects of W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3 are in an exploratory or developing phase and will change substantially. ... The final requirements in WCAG 3 will be different from this draft.

claims.claim: WCAG 3 replaces WCAG 2's pass/fail A/AA/AAA success-criteria conformance model with a fundamentally different conformance model intended to be more flexible for organizations.
claims.quote: The conformance model in WCAG 3 will be very different from WCAG 2

claims.claim: WCAG 3's scope is deliberately broader than web content, covering apps, tools, publishing, and emerging technologies — hence the name change from 'Web Content Accessibility Guidelines' to 'W3C Accessibility Guidelines'.
claims.quote: WCAG 3 applies to web content, apps, tools, publishing, and emerging technologies on the web.

claims.claim: Apple requires that on iOS the accessible label of a custom control must NOT contain the control's type or state — type and state must instead be supplied through the traits API (UIAccessibilityTraits) — otherwise VoiceOver double-speaks. This is the iOS analogue of the web rule against baking role/state into an accessible name, and it is a design-time naming decision.
claims.quote: Ensure that labels don't include control types like "checkbox" or states like "checked." Otherwise, VoiceOver may speak redundant information to the user, such as "Unsubscribe checkbox, checkbox." Instead, implement these in your app as traits or through similar APIs appropriate to the device.

claims.claim: Apple makes focus placement on screen/modal change an explicit evaluation criterion for iOS: when a screen changes or a modal appears, the VoiceOver cursor must move logically into the new content, and background/offscreen content must be unreachable. This mirrors the SPA route-change focus-management problem but is a platform requirement rather than a WCAG SC.
claims.quote: When the screen changes or a modal dialog appears, the VoiceOver cursor should move logically into the new content area. VoiceOver users shouldn't be able to move into invisible, offscreen, or background content.

claims.claim: The iOS equivalent of a web aria-live region is AccessibilityNotification: Apple specifies that temporary status banners and important in-app alerts be announced "in a timely but non-disruptive manner" via that API, rather than through any markup-level live-region concept.
claims.quote: Temporary status banners and important in-app alerts should be conveyed to VoiceOver users in a timely but non-disruptive manner, often done so with an AccessibilityNotification.

claims.claim: Apple states custom (non-native) elements must deliver accessibility equivalent to native UIKit, AppKit and SwiftUI controls — the iOS counterpart of the web's "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" / use-the-native-element rule, making the build-vs-use-native-control choice a concept-time decision.
claims.quote: Custom elements, if used by the app or any included frameworks, should provide equivalent accessibility of native elements provided by the Apple UIKit, AppKit, and SwiftUI frameworks. For example, custom buttons, tab bars, and sliders should be operable with VoiceOver and convey the same information as controls using standard API equivalents.

claims.claim: Apple gates a public App Store "Supports VoiceOver" declaration (Accessibility Nutrition Labels) on a task-completion standard, not a checklist of attributes: every common task in the app must be completable using VoiceOver alone without sighted assistance. This is a distribution-level enforcement mechanism with no direct web equivalent.
claims.quote: You may indicate your app supports VoiceOver if users are able to navigate and interact with visual elements, including text, media, buttons, and controls, using only VoiceOver. Using gestures or keyboard commands, users should be able to focus on each part of the UI, hear what it is, and activate it. Make sure users can complete all of the common tasks of your app using only VoiceOver, without sighted assistance.

claims.claim: Apple sets platform-specific control size targets that are stricter than WCAG 2.2's 2.5.8 minimum (24x24 CSS px): iOS/iPadOS default 44x44 pt with an absolute minimum of 28x28 pt; macOS 28x28 / 20x20 pt; tvOS 66x66 / 56x56 pt; visionOS 60x60 / 28x28 pt; watchOS 44x44 / 28x28 pt. This is a layout decision that must be made at design time, not audited after build.
claims.quote: Offer sufficiently sized controls. Controls that are too small are hard for many people to interact with and select. Strive to meet the recommended minimum control size for each platform to ensure controls and menus are comfortable for all when tapping and clicking. [Table — Platform / Default control size / Minimum control size: iOS, iPadOS 44x44 pt / 28x28 pt; macOS 28x28 pt / 20x20 pt; tvOS 66x66 pt / 56x56 pt; visionOS 60x60 pt / 28x28 pt; watchOS 44x44 pt / 28x28 pt]

claims.claim: Apple treats inter-control spacing as a first-class accessibility requirement separate from target size, and gives concrete numbers: roughly 12 pt of padding around bezeled elements and roughly 24 pt around the visible edges of unbezeled elements. WCAG 2.5.8 has no equivalent numeric spacing rule (it only offers spacing as an exception path), so native and web diverge here.
claims.quote: Consider spacing between controls as important as size. Include enough padding between elements to reduce the chance that someone taps the wrong control. In general, it works well to add about 12 points of padding around elements that include a bezel. For elements without a bezel, about 24 points of padding works well around the element's visible edges.

claims.claim: Apple explicitly adopts WCAG Level AA contrast values as its guidance and publishes them in point sizes rather than CSS px: 4.5:1 for text up to 17 pt at any weight, 3:1 at 18 pt at any weight, and 3:1 for bold text at all sizes. It also names APCA as a second recognized measure, and requires that apps failing the default minimum at least supply a higher-contrast scheme under the system Increase Contrast setting.
claims.quote: Strive to meet color contrast minimum standards... Two popular standards of measure for color contrast are the [WCAG] and the Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm (APCA)... uses the following values from WCAG Level AA as guidance in determining whether your app's colors have an acceptable contrast.
