[Table — Text size / Text weight / Minimum contrast ratio: Up to 17 pts / All / 4.5:1; 18 pts / All / 3:1; All / Bold / 3:1] If your app doesn't provide this minimum contrast by default, ensure it at least provides a higher contrast color scheme when the system setting Increase Contrast is turned on.

claims.claim: Apple's text-scaling target is 200 percent enlargement (140 percent on watchOS), satisfiable either by adopting Dynamic Type or by building custom scaling UI — and it publishes per-platform default and minimum type sizes (iOS/iPadOS 17 pt default / 11 pt minimum; macOS 13/10; tvOS 29/23; visionOS 17/12; watchOS 16/12) that custom type styles are expected to respect.
claims.quote: Support larger text sizes. Make sure people can adjust the size of your text or icons to make them more legible, visible, and comfortable to read. Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent (or 140 percent in watchOS apps). Your interface can support font size enlargement either through custom UI, or by adopting Dynamic Type. [Table — Platform / Default size / Minimum size: iOS, iPadOS 17 pt / 11 pt; macOS 13 pt / 10 pt; tvOS 29 pt / 23 pt; visionOS 17 pt / 12 pt; watchOS 16 pt / 12 pt]

claims.claim: Apple specifies concrete motion-design substitutions that must be decided when the animation is designed, not retrofitted: under Reduce Motion, tighten springs to cut bounce, track animation to gesture, avoid z-axis depth animation, replace x/y/z transitions with fades, and avoid animating into and out of blurs. It also requires apps to honor the system Dim Flashing Lights setting for video playback.
claims.quote: Other best practices for reducing motion include: Tightening animation springs to reduce bounce effects; Tracking animations directly with people's gestures; Avoiding animating depth changes in z-axis layers; Replacing transitions in x-, y-, and z-axes with fades to avoid motion; Avoiding animating into and out of blurs

result.publishDate: Last updated June 9, 2025 (per the page's own change log; prior substantive revision March 7, 2025, which moved Dynamic Type guidance to the Typography page and VoiceOver guidance to a separate VoiceOver page)

claims.claim: WCAG 3.0 as of 3 March 2026 is an informative W3C Draft Note, not a normative standard — its structure, guidelines, and conformance model are all still in draft, so it cannot be used as a compliance target today.
claims.quote: "This is an updated draft of the WCAG 3 Explainer. It is informative, not normative, and is not expected to become a W3C Recommendation." ... "The structure, guidelines, and conformance model are still in draft."

claims.claim: WCAG 3.0 will not be published until its coverage is at least equal to WCAG 2.2, and it does not deprecate WCAG 2 — meaning WCAG 2.2 remains the operative design and conformance target for the foreseeable future.
claims.quote: "WCAG 3 will not be published until it covers at least as much as WCAG 2.2." ... "It does not deprecate WCAG 2."

claims.claim: WCAG 3.0 introduces 'Assertions' as a normative conformance component: documented statements about the procedures practiced during development and evaluation (accessibility training, staffing, usability testing, heuristic evaluation, AT testing) — making design-time and organizational process, not just the built artifact, part of conformance.
claims.quote: "An Assertion is an attributable and documented statement of fact regarding procedures practiced in the development and maintenance of the content or product." ... "Examples of procedures that may be used during implementation might include: Accessibility training, FTE assignments, Skills testing." ... "Examples of procedures that may be used to evaluate accessibility might include: Usability testing, Heuristic evaluation, Testing with assistive technology."

claims.claim: WCAG 3.0 replaces the WCAG 2.x A/AA/AAA model with a three-tier Bronze/Silver/Gold conformance model built on Core Requirements plus varying portions of Supplemental Requirements and Assertions, and adds qualitative (non-binary) test types alongside reliably-repeatable ones.
claims.quote: Proposed three-tier model—Bronze (minimum), Silver (higher), and Gold (highest)—based on meeting all Core Requirements plus varying portions of Supplemental Requirements and Assertions. Test types include "Tests where there is a high degree of reliability between test results from different testers" and "Tests that rely on a qualitative evaluation based on existing criteria."

claims.claim: WCAG 3.0's scope expands beyond WCAG 2.x web content to cover XR (augmented, virtual, and mixed reality), voice input, publishing requirements, and guidance for authoring tools, user agents, and assistive technologies.
claims.quote: WCAG 3 will "address more disability needs than WCAG 2, incorporate publishing requirements and emerging technologies such as XR (augmented, virtual, and mixed reality) and voice input" and include guidance for authoring tools, user agents, and assistive technologies.

claims.claim: The DOJ ADA Title II web rule adopts WCAG 2.1 Level AA — not WCAG 2.2 — as the binding technical standard for state and local government web content and mobile apps, meaning the six success criteria added in WCAG 2.2 (2.4.11, 2.4.12, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8) are not themselves legally required by this US rule.
claims.quote: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) Version 2.1, Level AA is the technical standard for state and local governments' web content and mobile apps.

claims.claim: Compliance deadlines are tiered by population: entities serving 50,000 or more persons must comply by April 26, 2027; entities serving 0 to 49,999 persons and special district governments must comply by April 26, 2028. The rule itself was published April 24, 2024.
claims.quote: 50,000 or more persons — April 26, 2027 | 0 to 49,999 persons — April 26, 2028 | Special district governments — April 26, 2028

claims.claim: Native mobile apps are covered by the same WCAG 2.1 Level AA obligation as web content, with the rule defining mobile apps as downloadable software for smartphones and tablets — so the standard is applied to iOS/Android platforms whose native accessibility APIs (VoiceOver, TalkBack, Dynamic Type) are the actual implementation surface.
claims.quote: State and local governments' mobile apps usually need to meet WCAG 2.1, Level AA … software applications that are downloaded and designed to run on mobile devices like smartphones and tablets

claims.claim: The rule provides five enumerated exceptions to the WCAG 2.1 AA requirement: archived web content, preexisting electronic documents (word processing, presentation, PDF, spreadsheet), third-party/user-generated content, password-protected individualized documents about a specific person, property, or account, and preexisting social media posts.
claims.quote: Archived content … Preexisting documents (word processing, presentation, PDF, or spreadsheet files posted before compliance date) … Third-party posts (user-generated content only) … Password-protected individualized documents … Preexisting social media posts

claims.claim: The rule includes a de minimis nonconformance defense and preserves the fundamental alteration / undue burden limits, but even where those apply the entity must still deliver effective communication, reasonable modifications, and equal opportunity to participate — i.e. conformance failures are not a blanket excuse from access obligations.
claims.quote: state and local governments may be able to show that their web content or mobile apps do not meet WCAG Version 2.1, Level AA in a way that is so minor that it would not change a person with a disability's access to the content or mobile app

claims.claim: DOJ's April 20, 2026 Interim Final Rule pushed both ADA Title II web/mobile-app compliance dates back by one year: entities with population 50,000+ move from April 24, 2026 to April 26, 2027, and entities under 50,000 plus all special district governments move from April 26, 2027 to April 26, 2028.
claims.quote: The compliance date for State and local government entities with a total population of 50,000 or more is extended from April 24, 2026, to April 26, 2027. The compliance date for public entities with a total population of less than 50,000, or any special district government, is extended from April 26, 2027, to April 26, 2028.

claims.claim: The ADA Title II rule's binding technical standard is WCAG 2.1 Level AA as published June 5, 2018 — a static version — and DOJ states explicitly that WCAG 2.2 is NOT incorporated by the rule, so the 2.2-only criteria (2.5.7, 2.5.8, 2.4.11, 2.4.12, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8) are not legally required under Title II.
claims.quote: the rule adopted the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (``WCAG'') version 2.1 Level AA (hereinafter referred to as ``WCAG 2.1''), published in June 2018, as the technical standard for web content and mobile app accessibility under title II. ... that link often takes the user to a web page discussing the WCAG 2.2 standards, which is a newer standard not incorporated by the 2024 rule.

claims.claim: The extension does not suspend or reduce any underlying accessibility obligation — public entities remain bound by Title II for web content and mobile apps during the extension period, and the IFR changes only timing, not substance.
claims.quote: Regardless of the compliance dates, covered entities have an ongoing obligation to ensure that their services, programs, and activities offered using web content and mobile apps are accessible to individuals with disabilities in accordance with their existing obligations under title II of the ADA.

claims.claim: DOJ signals the substantive content of the 2024 rule is itself unsettled: it plans further rulemaking and may issue an NPRM during the extension period to reopen the rule's substance, but absent that it anticipates the rule taking effect at the new deadlines.
claims.quote: While this IFR is limited to extending the 2024 final rule's compliance dates, the Department plans to engage in future rulemaking processes related to the substantive requirements of the 2024 final rule. During the extension period, the Department will consider issuing an NPRM providing members of the public with an opportunity to comment on the substance of the 2024 final rule and any changes proposed by the Department. If the Department does not issue such an NPRM and if circumstances suggesting further delays of this deadline do not exist, the Department fully anticipates implementing the regulation at the new deadline.

claims.claim: The extension took legal effect immediately on publication (April 20, 2026, cited as 91 FR 20902) as an interim final rule issued under the APA good-cause exception, with comments accepted only afterward through June 22, 2026 — meaning the new deadlines were operative before any public comment was considered.
claims.quote: ACTION: Interim final rule; request for comments. ... Effective date: This IFR is effective April 20, 2026. Comments: Written comments must be submitted on or before June 22, 2026.

claims.claim: EN 301 549 — the harmonised standard that creates a presumption of conformity with EAA obligations — currently builds on WCAG 2.1, but a draft version 4.1.0 was published in November 2025 with an approved version expected in the EU Official Journal in Q3 2026, and version 4.1.1 is expected to reference WCAG 2.2. Designers of EU-facing digital products should therefore already be designing to WCAG 2.2.
claims.quote: The central standard for digital accessibility is EN 301 549 . At present, EN 301 549 largely builds on the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines WCAG 2.1 ... A first draft of version 4.1.0 was published in November 2025, and an approved version is expected to be published in the Official Journal of the EU in Q3 2026. The forthcoming version 4.1.1 is expected to reference WCAG 2.2 , meaning businesses should already plan for an evolution beyond WCAG 2.1 when designing or upgrading their digital offerings.

claims.claim: In a landmark interim ruling of 4 June 2026, the Judicial Court of Caen held that Carrefour's e-commerce site and app breached French digital accessibility obligations despite 71.21% conformity with EN 301 549 (measured via RGAA), rejected a 'global' functional-usability assessment in favour of criterion-by-criterion assessment against perceivable/operable/understandable/robust, and ordered conformity within six months subject to a EUR 500/day penalty plus EUR 10,000 provisional damages.
claims.quote: Relying on Carrefour's own accessibility audit, which showed 71.21% conformity with the reference standard EN 301 549 by assessment through the RGAA framework ... the court held that significant remaining barriers (including missing or inadequate alternative texts for images, insufficient colour contrast, poorly labelled links, incompatibility with assistive technologies and misuse of HTML semantics) prevent visually impaired users from fully using the service. The court rejected Carrefour's argument that accessibility should be assessed solely on the basis of whether persons with disabilities are effectively able to use the service ... The court emphasized that "it is clear that the e-commerce website cannot be merely a little accessible, it must be fully accessible". Carrefour has been ordered to bring its e - commerce services into conformity, subject to a penalty payment of EUR 500 per day if full compliance is not achieved within six months of the order.

claims.claim: Germany's EAA market surveillance authority, the MLBF, formally began operations on 26 September 2025 and applies a graduated enforcement model — correction orders, then restriction or prohibition of the product or service, with administrative fines of up to EUR 100,000 — and by mid-2026 has moved from set-up to concrete supervisory activity, sending follow-up questions to providers that self-reported partial non-compliance in 2025.
claims.quote: The MLBF formally started operations on 26 September 2025 ... Correction orders : Providers are first required to remedy formal or material non‑conformities within a set deadline. Restrictions and prohibitions : If non‑compliance persists, the authority can restrict or prohibit the offer or provision of services or the placing of products on the market. Administrative fines : breaches can trigger fines of up to EUR 100,000.

claims.claim: The MLBF's published market surveillance strategy uses automated technical testing tools to screen web-based services proactively, prioritising by factors including user reach, monopoly position, complexity and interactivity of the service, and relevance for autonomous living — meaning in-scope digital services are subject to systematic automated regulatory scanning rather than complaint-only enforcement.
claims.quote: Web‑based services are screened through technical testing tools, allowing the authority to cover a broader range of offerings than would be possible with purely manual checks. The MLBF intends to prioritize services and products that are essential for everyday participation and that have significant market coverage.

claims.claim: The EAA has no GDPR-style one-stop-shop: each Member State designates its own market surveillance authority, so non-conformity notifications (Art. 13(4) EAA / Sec. 14(4) BFSG) and exemption notifications for fundamental alteration or disproportionate burden (Art. 14 EAA / Sec. 16, 17 BFSG) must be filed separately in every Member State where the service is provided.
claims.quote: Unlike the GDPR, the EAA does likely not establish a one - stop - shop mechanism. Each Member State designates its own market surveillance authority (or authorities) with national competence ... Exemption notifications (for fundamental alteration or disproportionate burden under Art. 14 EAA (Sec. 16, 17 BFSG) likewise must be submitted individually to each Member State in which the operator relies on the exception.

claims.claim: EN 301 549 V3.2.1 pins its web accessibility requirements to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, not WCAG 2.2 — the six criteria new in WCAG 2.2 (2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size Minimum, 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication) appear nowhere in the document, so as of this version EU-harmonised conformance does not demand them.
claims.quote: Conformance with W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.1) [5] Level AA is equivalent to conforming with all of clauses 9.1 to 9.4 and the conformance requirements of clause 9.6 of the present document.

claims.claim: EN 301 549 is a harmonised standard whose legal force is a 'presumption of conformity': meeting the normative clauses listed in Annex A Tables A.1 and A.2 is deemed to satisfy the essential requirements of Directive 2016/2102 (the Web Accessibility Directive) once the standard is cited in the Official Journal of the EU.
claims.quote: Once the present document is cited in the Official Journal of the European Union under Directive 2016/2102 [i.28], conformance with the normative clauses of the present document given in Tables A.1 and A.2 confers, within the limits of the scope of the present document, a presumption of conformity with the corresponding essential requirements of that Directive and associated EFTA regulations.

claims.claim: Native mobile applications are covered by clause 11 (Software), not clause 9 (Web), and clause 11.5.2.3 makes use of the platform's documented accessibility services a mandatory ('shall') requirement — i.e. a native iOS/Android app must route its UI through UIAccessibility/VoiceOver and the Android accessibility framework/TalkBack rather than inventing its own mechanism; Annex A Table A.2 is the mobile-application counterpart to the web table.
claims.quote: Where the software provides a user interface it shall use the applicable documented platform accessibility services. If the documented platform accessibility services do not allow the software to meet the applicable requirements of clauses 11.5.2.5 to 11.5.2.17, then software that provides a user interface shall use other documented services to interoperate with assistive technology.

claims.claim: For non-web software (including mobile apps), clause 11.5.2.5 requires that every UI element expose role, states, boundary, name and description programmatically to assistive technology — the native-platform equivalent of the web's accessible-name/role/value contract, making accessible names for custom controls a normative requirement rather than a best practice.
claims.quote: Where the software provides a user interface it shall, by using the services as described in clause 11.5.2.3, make the user interface elements' role, state(s), boundary, name, and description programmatically determinable by assistive technologies.

claims.claim: The standard imposes explicit focus-tracking and change-notification duties on non-web software (clauses 11.5.2.13 and 11.5.2.15) — the native analogue of web focus management on view change and aria-live announcements for async updates — requiring the app to both expose focus/selection state and actively notify assistive technologies when those attributes change.
claims.quote: Where software provides a user interface it shall, by using the services as described in clause 11.5.2.3, notify assistive technologies about changes in those programmatically determinable attributes of user interface elements that are referenced in requirements 11.5.2.5 to 11.5.2.11 and 11.5.2.13.

claims.claim: The European Accessibility Act's obligations became applicable on 28 June 2025: Member States had to adopt transposing law by 28 June 2022 and apply those measures from 28 June 2025 (with an optional derogation to 28 June 2027 only for the '112' emergency-call obligations in Article 4(8)).
claims.quote: Article 31 Transposition — 1. Member States shall adopt and publish, by 28 June 2022, the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive. […] 2. They shall apply those measures from 28 June 2025. 3. By way of derogation from paragraph 2 of this Article, Member States may decide to apply the measures regarding the obligations set out in Article 4(8) at the latest from 28 June 2027.

claims.claim: Article 2 binds the EAA to mainstream digital interfaces, not just hardware: it covers e-commerce services, consumer banking services, e-books and dedicated software, electronic communications services, and the websites, mobile apps, e-ticketing and self-service terminals of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport — for services provided to consumers after 28 June 2025.
claims.quote: 2. Without prejudice to Article 32, this Directive applies to the following services provided to consumers after 28 June 2025: (a) electronic communications services […] (c) the following elements of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport services […] (i) websites; (ii) mobile device-based services including mobile applications; (iii) electronic tickets and electronic ticketing services […] (d) consumer banking services; (e) e-books and dedicated software; and (f) e-commerce services.

claims.claim: Annex I Section III writes the WCAG POUR principles into binding EU law for service interfaces: websites, their online applications, and mobile device-based services including mobile applications must be made accessible 'in a consistent and adequate way by making them perceivable, operable, understandable and robust' — making conformance a design-time requirement, not an optional guideline.
claims.quote: (c) making websites, including the related online applications, and mobile device-based services, including mobile applications, accessible in a consistent and adequate way by making them perceivable, operable, understandable and robust;

claims.claim: Compliance is proved through harmonised standards: products and services conforming to harmonised standards whose references are published in the Official Journal are presumed to conform to the EAA's accessibility requirements — the legal mechanism by which EN 301 549 (and through it WCAG) confers presumption of conformity.
claims.quote: Article 15 Presumption of conformity — 1. Products and services which are in conformity with harmonised standards or parts thereof the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, shall be presumed to be in conformity with the accessibility requirements of this Directive in so far as those standards or parts thereof cover those requirements.

claims.claim: Article 32 grants transitional relief that softens the 2025 cliff edge: service providers may keep using products lawfully used before 28 June 2025 until 28 June 2030, pre-2025 service contracts may run unaltered for up to five more years, and existing self-service terminals may stay in service for up to 20 years after entry into use.
claims.quote: Article 32 Transitional measures — 1. […] Member States shall provide for a transitional period ending on 28 June 2030 during which service providers may continue to provide their services using products which were lawfully used by them to provide similar services before that date. Service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 may continue without alteration until they expire, but no longer than five years from that date. 2. Member States may provide that self-service terminals lawfully used by service providers […] before 28 June 2025 may continue to be used […] but no longer than 20 years after their entry into use.

result.publishDate: 2019-06-07 (Official Journal of the European Union L 151/70, 7.6.2019; Directive adopted 17 April 2019)

result.evidence:
The claim misstates the normative text of the very source it cites, and the "supporting quote" does not appear in WCAG 2.2 at all.

1) VERBATIM SC 3.3.8 (W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024, https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ and https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html): "A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of the following: **Alternative** — Another authentication method that does not rely on a cognitive function test. **Mechanism** — A mechanism is available to assist the user in completing the cognitive function test. **Object Recognition** — The cognitive function test is to recognize objects. **Personal Content** — The cognitive function test is to identify non-text content the user provided to the website." Note 2: "Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of re-typing."

2) FABRICATED "ESSENTIAL" EXCEPTION. WebFetch of the W3C Understanding page explicitly confirms the SC statement "does not include the word 'essential' or any phrase like 'except where that test is essential.'" The word does not appear in 3.3.8 in any published version; searches for that wording in WCAG 2.2 drafts return nothing. "Essential" is an exception clause borrowed from other criteria (e.g. 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size Minimum) — cross-contamination, not 3.3.8. The claim's core structural framing ("forbids ... unless essential") is therefore wrong.

3) TWO OF FOUR EXCEPTIONS OMITTED — and this is designer-material, not pedantic. The claim asserts "only object-recognition and personal-content exceptions," dropping **Alternative** and **Mechanism**, which are the two exceptions a designer actually uses to pass. This makes the claim internally self-contradictory: it says password auth is ruled out "without paste/password-manager support," but paste/password-manager support IS the Mechanism exception it just denied exists. Under the real SC, a memorized-password login conforms at AA whenever paste/password-manager entry is supported or a non-cognitive alternative (passkey, magic link, OAuth) is offered — the criterion does not require the test to be "essential."

4) Also note AAA 3.3.9 (Enhanced) removes Object Recognition and Personal Content but *retains* Alternative and Mechanism — so neither the AA nor the AAA level has an "essential" carve-out, further confirming the claim's rule-shape is invented.

What survives: the underlying design consequences are directionally right (text/transcription CAPTCHA as sole path fails; password-manager/paste support is required if passwords are the only method; object-recognition CAPTCHAs are excepted at AA). But the claim as written misquotes the primary source, invents an exception, and omits half the conformance paths — a designer following it would wrongly conclude that supporting paste cannot make a password flow conformant. Per the checklist ("unsupported by quote / overreach / misread"), refuted.

The normative text at #dragging-movements reads verbatim: "All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the functionality is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author." Markup confirms `

(Level AA)

` and `

New

`. WCAG 2.2 is a current W3C Recommendation (last updated 12 Dec 2024); 2.5.7 is unchanged. So the claim's substance — AA, single-pointer non-drag alternative required unless essential, and therefore a concept-stage decision — holds. TWO DEFECTS that must be corrected before the claim is used, neither fatal: 1. The "supporting quote" is NOT verbatim from the cited primary source. The claim quotes "Functionality that can be operated by dragging movements can also be operated by single pointer actions without dragging, unless dragging is essential." That string does not appear in WCAG 2.2. It is a paraphrase that silently drops the SECOND exception: "or the functionality is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author." Citing it as a primary-source quote is a citation error. 2. That dropped exception directly bites one of the claim's own examples. "Every drag interaction ... map pan" is an overreach: browser-provided scrolling/panning (CSS overflow scroll, touch pan, pull-to-refresh) is exempt because it is user-agent determined. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/dragging-movements.html states the SC "does not apply to techniques such as CSS overflow that make a section of content scrollable, as the actual scrolling mechanism is provided by the user agent," and only applies "if content actively suppresses the user agent's own scrolling functionality and/or implements its own scrolling mechanism." A Leaflet/Google-Maps-style widget IS in scope (the Understanding doc lists "maps with directional buttons" as a sufficient example); native browser panning is not. "Drag-to-upload" is also not named in the Understanding examples — the WCAG definition of "dragging movement" requires the pointer to engage an element on the down-event, and an OS-desktop file drag begins outside the content; the click-to-browse file input is standard practice anyway, so the design advice is right for the wrong reason. Corroborating detail the claim omits but that strengthens the design-time framing: the Understanding doc states "achieving keyboard equivalence for a dragging operation does not automatically meet this success criterion, unless that equivalent keyboard operation also provides controls that can be clicked or tapped with a pointer." So a keyboard-only alternative fails 2.5.7 — the alternative must be pointer-operable, which is a visible-affordance (design) decision, not a code-time one. The claim's list of reorder lists, sliders, and kanban is directly supported: the Understanding doc's sufficient-technique examples include range sliders with click-anywhere tracks, sortable lists with up/down controls, and kanban widgets with arrow buttons. Verdict: not refuted. Restate with the full two-exception text and drop the unqualified "map pan"/"drag-to-upload" phrasing.

result.evidence:
The claim misstates the normative criterion, and its own cited primary source refutes it. Verbatim from https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#accessible-authentication-minimum (fetched 2026-07-28, extracted from the spec HTML):

"Success Criterion 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA) — A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of the following: **Alternative** — Another authentication method that does not rely on a cognitive function test. **Mechanism** — A mechanism is available to assist the user in completing the cognitive function test. **Object Recognition** — The cognitive function test is to recognize objects. **Personal Content** — The cognitive function test is to identify non-text content the user provided to the website."

Three defects:

(1) FABRICATED EXCEPTION. The claim says the test is forbidden "unless essential." The word "essential" appears ZERO times in SC 3.3.8 (and zero times in 3.3.9). There is no essential-exception escape hatch in this SC, unlike 1.4.5, 2.2.1, 2.5.7, etc. The "supporting quote" ("A mechanism is available that does not rely on cognitive function test to authenticate, except where that test is essential") is not verbatim W3C text — it welds the Mechanism and Alternative bullets together and appends an invented qualifier. The W3C Understanding page confirms "essential" does not appear in the SC text. Some vendor blogs (allaccessible.org, accessicart.com) propagate an "essential for high-security content" gloss; that is not in the normative or Understanding text.

(2) TWO OF FOUR SATISFYING CONDITIONS DROPPED. The claim asserts "only object-recognition and personal-content exceptions." There are four, and the two omitted ones (Alternative, Mechanism) are the primary compliance routes for designers. This inverts the design guidance: it implies a password login can only be made conformant by converting the test into object recognition or personal content, when in fact offering passkeys/SSO/email-link (Alternative) or supporting password managers and paste (Mechanism) is the normal answer. Proof these two are core, not incidental: the AAA sibling 3.3.9 strips Object Recognition and Personal Content but RETAINS Alternative and Mechanism.

(3) INTERNAL CONTRADICTION. The claim's own conclusion — that password memorization is impermissible "without paste/password-manager support" — is derived entirely from the Mechanism bullet it says does not exist. Note 2 of the SC states verbatim: "Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of re-typing."

What survives: Level AA is correct; "not required for any step in an authentication process" is correct; text-transcription CAPTCHA as a sole path does fail, since the glossary defines cognitive function test as "a task that requires the user to remember, manipulate, or transcribe information … transcription, such as typing in characters." But the claim also over-broadens "memorization": the same glossary entry carves out "The common identifiers name, e-mail, and phone number are not considered cognitive function tests as they are personal to the user and consistent across websites."

The practical conclusions are roughly right by accident; the rule as stated is wrong in a way that would mislead a designer using it as guidance.

VERBATIM normative text at #dragging-movements: "Success Criterion 2.5.7 Dragging Movements ... (Level AA) New — All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the functionality is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author. Note: This requirement applies to web content that interprets pointer actions (i.e., this does not apply to actions that are required to operate the user agent or assistive technology)." The spec's own conformance-level index also lists "2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA)". So: SC number, name, Level AA, "single pointer without dragging", and the "essential" exception are all exactly as claimed.

CORRECTION 1 — the supplied "supporting quote" is a paraphrase, not the source text. "Functionality that can be operated by dragging movements can also be operated by single pointer actions without dragging, unless dragging is essential" does not appear anywhere in WCAG 2.2. It must be replaced with the verbatim sentence above before publication, or the doc is misquoting a primary source it cites by URL.

CORRECTION 2 — the claim drops one of two normative exceptions, and that omission makes part of its example list wrong. The spec exempts functionality "determined by the user agent and not modified by the author." A native <input type="range"> slider is therefore exempt (browser supplies the thumb and its drag behaviour); only a custom div/pointer-event slider needs an author-supplied click-the-track or +/- stepper. Same for native file-input drop behaviour vs. an author-built dropzone — and drag-to-upload almost always already ships its non-drag alternative in the form of the "Browse" button that <input type="file"> renders. So "every drag interaction (… sliders … drag-to-upload) must be designed with a non-drag equivalent" over-reaches; the accurate framing is "every AUTHOR-IMPLEMENTED drag interaction." Reorder lists, kanban and map pan (all author-implemented) are correct as listed, and W3C's Understanding doc names exactly those cases (map arrow buttons, adjacent move controls / pop-up menus for lists and task boards).

Supporting, and strengthening the design-time framing: W3C's Understanding SC 2.5.7 states that satisfying the keyboard criteria (2.1.1 / 2.1.3) does NOT satisfy 2.5.7 — a drag UI that is keyboard-operable still fails without "controls that can be clicked or tapped with a pointer." That means the fix is a visible affordance (button, menu, track hit area) occupying real estate, which genuinely is a layout/concept-stage decision, not a post-build remediation. The "from the concept stage" inference is the claim's own editorial reasoning rather than normative text, but it follows.

No credible source disputes the core requirement. The only contrary noise I found was a secondary vendor blog asserting sliders on touch "count as a swipe gesture and are therefore exempt" — that confuses 2.5.7 with 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (path-based) and is not a W3C position; I give it no weight.

NET: core assertion is true, primary-sourced, current, Level AA correct. Not refuted. Ship it only after (a) replacing the fabricated quote with the verbatim sentence and (b) adding the user-agent exception, which changes "sliders" and "drag-to-upload" from unconditional obligations to conditional ones.

MISQUOTE + OVERREACH, though the core direction is right.

1) The "supporting quote" does not exist in the cited primary source. I downloaded https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ (512KB, /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-taha/a37ae9f9-eb70-4000-aa63-8f4f998a4172/scratchpad/wcag22.html) and grepped it. The string "single pointer actions" appears 0 times in the whole spec. "can also be operated" appears exactly once — in SC 2.5.4 Motion Actuation ("Functionality that can be operated by device motion or user motion can also be operated by user interface components..."). The claim's quote is a paraphrase built on 2.5.4's sentence pattern, presented as a verbatim W3C quotation. (Note: a first WebFetch of the TR page "confirmed" the quote verbatim — it hallucinated agreement with my prompt. Direct curl+grep contradicts it.)

2) Actual normative text of SC 2.5.7 (Level AA, New), extracted from the spec HTML: "All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential OR THE FUNCTIONALITY IS DETERMINED BY THE USER AGENT AND NOT MODIFIED BY THE AUTHOR." Plus a normative Note: "This requirement applies to web content that interprets pointer actions (i.e., this does not apply to actions that are required to operate the user agent or assistive technology)." The claim drops the second exception and the Note entirely.

3) That omission makes the claim's absolutist scope wrong on its own examples. Understanding SC 2.5.7 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/dragging-movements.html) states explicitly: "This criterion does not apply to scrolling and dragging gestures enabled by the user agent... This criterion also does not apply to the use of techniques such as CSS overflow that make a section of content scrollable... The criterion does apply if content actively suppresses the user agent's own scrolling functionality and/or implements its own scrolling mechanism." So "map pan" is only in scope when author-implemented, not when it is UA/CSS scrolling. And the spec's definition of "dragging movement" is "an operation where the pointer engages with an element on the down-event and the element (or a representation of its position) follows the pointer until an up-event" — dragging a file from the OS desktop into a drop zone starts outside the content, and the native <input type="file"> drop behavior is user-agent-determined, i.e. exempt. The claim's flat "every drag interaction (... map pan, drag-to-upload) must be designed with a non-drag equivalent" therefore overstates the SC.

4) What survives (so this is a fix, not a kill): SC 2.5.7 is genuinely Level AA and New in WCAG 2.2; the Understanding doc's "In Brief" is "Goal: Don't rely on dragging for user actions. What to do: For any action that involves dragging, provide a simple pointer alternative." Reorder lists, sliders, kanban, carousels are correctly in scope. One extra design-time point the claim misses and that matters more than what it says: "achieving keyboard equivalence for a dragging operation does not automatically meet this success criterion, unless that equivalent keyboard operation also provides controls that can be clicked or tapped with a pointer" — a keyboard-only fallback fails 2.5.7.

Corrected form the claim should take: "SC 2.5.7 (AA, new in 2.2) requires author-implemented drag functionality to also work via single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the behavior is user-agent-determined and unmodified (native scrolling, CSS overflow, drag-to-refresh, native file-input drop). Keyboard alternatives alone don't satisfy it — the alternative must be clickable/tappable."

WebFetch of https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ returns the normative text verbatim as quoted: SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA — "When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content." Levels (AA vs AAA) and the entirely-hidden vs any-part threshold split are exactly as claimed, no paraphrase drift.

The design implication is also W3C-supported, not the reviewer's extrapolation. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-not-obscured-minimum states "Typical types of content that can overlap focused items are sticky footers, sticky headers, and non-modal dialogs" and "A notification implemented as sticky content, such as a cookie banner, will fail this success criterion if it entirely obscures a component receiving focus," and confirms the AA/AAA relationship: "For best visibility, none of the component receiving focus should be obscured. This preferred outcome is covered by the AAA criterion." There is a dedicated W3C failure technique F110 ("Failure of SC 2.4.11 ... due to a sticky footer or header completely hiding focused elements"). Chatbots/expandable side nav are named in the Understanding doc as more complex cases.

CURRENCY CHECK: WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation (5 Oct 2023, updated 12 Dec 2024). The WCAG 2.2 errata page shows the 2024-11-19 and 2025-06-27 entries touch 2.5.8 exception formatting and the perimeter/single-pointer definitions — nothing altering 2.4.11 or 2.4.12 normative text. No contradicting source found; every result (W3C, TestParty, AAArdvark, AccessiTREE, a11y-blog) states the same threshold split.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS that do not rise to refutation:
(1) The claim omits 2.4.11's two normative notes: only the initial positions of user-repositionable content are tested, and user-opened content that the user can reveal without advancing keyboard focus is not treated as obscuring. This matters specifically for the "floating chat widgets" example — a user-opened chat panel can be exempt under Note 2; a persistent or auto-opening bubble is not. The claim overgeneralizes chat widgets slightly.
(2) "Must be sized and positioned against these thresholds at layout time" presents layout geometry as the sole remedy. W3C also allows scroll-padding/scroll-margin, making the banner modal so it must be dismissed, or closing the notification on loss of focus. These are still concept/design-time decisions, so the claim's thrust (decide at design time, not audit after) holds; only the "sized and positioned" framing is narrower than the spec's remedy set.

(1) THE SUPPORTING QUOTE IS FABRICATED. The claim attributes to w3.org: "A mechanism is available that does not rely on cognitive function test to authenticate, except where that test is essential." No such sentence exists in SC 3.3.8. A regex scan for "essential" across the entire 3.3.8 section of the Recommendation returns ZERO hits. "Essential" is a WCAG defined term, but it scopes other SCs (2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions, 3.2.5 Change on Request) — never 3.3.8. There is no "unless essential" escape hatch in Accessible Authentication.

(2) THE EXCEPTION SET IS WRONG — AND NEARLY INVERTED. Verbatim normative text: "A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of the following: [Alternative] Another authentication method that does not rely on a cognitive function test. [Mechanism] A mechanism is available to assist the user in completing the cognitive function test. [Object Recognition] The cognitive function test is to recognize objects. [Personal Content] The cognitive function test is to identify non-text content the user provided to the website."

That is FOUR bullets. The claim asserts "only object-recognition and personal-content exceptions," omitting Alternative and Mechanism — the two most designer-load-bearing paths. The claim has it backwards: it is 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced), Level AAA, that DROPS Object Recognition and Personal Content while RETAINING Alternative and Mechanism. The claim describes roughly the complement of the real AA exception set.

(3) INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT. The claim's own conclusion — that mandating password memorization "without paste/password-manager support" fails — derives solely from the Mechanism bullet it just denied exists. Note 2 of the SC states it explicitly: "Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of re-typing." A password field passes 3.3.8 via Mechanism (paste + autofill support), not via object recognition or personal content.

PARTIALLY CORRECT ELEMENTS (insufficient to save it): Level AA is right; SC 3.3.8 is new in 2.2; the downstream verdicts (paste-blocking fails — see failure technique F109 "preventing password or code re-entry in the same format"; a transcription-based text CAPTCHA as sole login path fails) are directionally correct. But they are correct in spite of the stated rule, not because of it. A designer applying the rule AS WRITTEN would (a) wrongly believe an "essential" business-justification defense exists, and (b) wrongly believe a standard password login can only conform through object recognition or user-supplied personal content. Both errors are material at design time — which is precisely the use context of the research question.

Not an outdated-source problem: WCAG 2.2 has been a W3C Recommendation since Oct 2023 (editorially updated Dec 2024) and the 3.3.8 text is unchanged. The source (w3.org) is maximal quality; the failure is that the claim misreads and misquotes it. A build check CAN detect the violation; what it cannot do is decide the layout. Read as "detection is impossible", the tail is wrong; read as "the fix is a comp-level layout decision", it holds. The cited URL (WAI Understanding index) is a weaker pointer than the normative https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#target-size-minimum, but the quoted string appears verbatim in the Recommendation itself, which I retrieved directly. 2. "conventional password-plus-CAPTCHA login flows fail" is the inverse of W3C's own statement. Understanding SC 3.3.8, "Login forms" section: "Websites can use username (or email) and password inputs as an authentication method if the author enables the user agent (browser) and any third-party password managers to fill in the fields." Failure is scoped narrowly: "However, if user agents and password managers are actively blocked from filling in the fields ... or users are prevented from copy and paste operations ... then the page would fail this criterion unless an alternative is provided." So a conventional password login PASSES by default; it fails only when paste/autofill is blocked or the input format differs from the stored format (cf. failure technique F109; per-digit OTP boxes; "enter the 1st, 3rd and 5th character").
3. The CAPTCHA half is also over-generalized. Understanding 3.3.8: "While recognizing objects, or a picture the user has previously provided, are cognitive function tests, these are excepted in this criterion at AA level." Image object-recognition CAPTCHAs pass at AA; distorted-text CAPTCHAs and puzzle CAPTCHAs fail, and an audio alternative that must be transcribed does not rescue them ("If the user needs to transcribe this audio, it cannot be used to meet the Alternative exception").
4. The claim omits a normative carve-out that is material at design time: the glossary explicitly says "The common identifiers name, e-mail, and phone number are not considered cognitive function tests as they are personal to the user and consistent across websites."
5. The supporting quote is a splice: the first half is the SC text, the second half is the separate glossary definition of "cognitive function test," joined by an ellipsis as if continuous. Both fragments are individually verbatim, but the composite misrepresents document structure.

Net effect for the research deliverable: as written, the claim would tell a designer that passwords must be replaced to reach AA. W3C's position is the opposite — keep the password, do not block paste, expose autocomplete/Input Purpose (1.3.5) and proper accessible names (4.1.2) so password managers can fill, never require transcription of an OTP, and if you use a CAPTCHA make it object recognition rather than character transcription or a puzzle. Corrected formulation: "3.3.8 (AA) forbids *requiring* a cognitive function test at any authentication step unless the step satisfies Alternative, Mechanism, Object Recognition, or Personal Content; ordinary password login satisfies Mechanism as long as autofill and paste are not blocked."

Attempted refutation on five fronts; the factual core survives all of them.

1) SOURCE VERIFICATION (primary, verbatim). W3C Understanding SC 2.5.8 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html) gives the normative text: "The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when:" followed by five exceptions, the first being Spacing: "Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target." So the number (24x24), the unit (CSS pixels), and the size-OR-spacing structure in the claim are all exactly right. Level confirmed AA in https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/.

2) NOT OUTDATED. WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation, second edition dated 12 December 2024; the 24x24 figure and the five exceptions are unchanged in the current text I fetched today. No superseding version exists (WCAG 3.0 remains a Working Draft).

3) NOT A MARKETING/SECONDARY CLAIM. The threshold comes straight from the normative spec, not a vendor blog.

4) TWO REAL QUALIFICATIONS FOUND, neither fatal to the claim as worded:
   (a) The claim compresses five exceptions into one. Besides Spacing, the spec also exempts Equivalent (same function available via a conforming control on the page), Inline ("The target is in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text" — this exempts in-sentence text links, a real designer-facing carve-out the claim never mentions), User agent control, and Essential. The claim's "must be at least 24x24 ... or else have sufficient spacing" is therefore incomplete, but it is not false — and the cited WAI page itself uses the same two-path plain-language summary ("Ensure targets meet a minimum size or have sufficient spacing around them").
   (b) "Sufficient spacing" is looser than the spec: the actual test is a geometric one (24px-diameter circles centered on each undersized target's bounding box must not intersect), which is satisfiable by offset/position, not only by literal padding. A design token for "tap spacing" is a fair operationalization but does not fully encode the circle test.

5) THE WEAKEST PART IS THE FRAMING CLAUSE, "rather than a post-build audit item." This is a false dichotomy: 2.5.8 is in fact one of the few WCAG 2.2 criteria that automates well, and Deque built an axe-core `target-size` rule specifically for it (https://dequeuniversity.com/rules/axe/4.9/target-size), noting it is likely the only new WCAG 2.2 rule axe-core will add because the others produce too many false positives. So it is both a design-time spec AND a post-build automated check. Also worth flagging: 24px is a floor far below Apple HIG's 44pt and Material's 48dp touch-target guidance, so treating 24 as the design-system token would meet WCAG AA while being poor mobile design. These qualify the editorial framing; they do not contradict the substantive, primary-sourced assertion that 2.5.8 fixes a concrete 24x24 CSS-pixel number a designer can spec at layout time.

Recommended wording fix before use: say "at least 24x24 CSS pixels unless one of five exceptions applies (spacing per the 24px-circle test, equivalent control, inline text links, user-agent-controlled, or essential)" and drop "rather than a post-build audit item" in favor of "in addition to being one of the few WCAG 2.2 criteria that automated tooling can check."

1. VERBATIM CHECK against the normative spec (not just the quote). Downloaded https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ (512KB) and extracted the 2.5.8 block programmatically. Exact text: "Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) ... (Level AA) New — The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when: Spacing ... Equivalent ... Inline ... User Agent Control ... Essential ...". Level AA and the 24x24 CSS pixel figure are confirmed verbatim, and the spec itself tags it "New" (i.e. added over 2.1).

2. MEASUREMENT METHOD confirmed verbatim in the Understanding doc under the heading "Size requirement": "For a target to be 'at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels', it must be conceptually possible to draw a solid 24 by 24 CSS pixel square, aligned to the horizontal and vertical axis such that the square is completely within the target (does not extend outside the target's area)." The claim's phrasing of this is accurate and correctly scoped to measuring "at least 24 by 24", not to overall conformance.

3. CURRENCY. WCAG 2.2 current version is "W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024" — still current as of July 2026. The W3C errata page lists exactly one erratum touching 2.5.8: 2024-11-19, "updating formatting, grammar, and punctuation of exceptions" (w3c/wcag PR #3189) — purely editorial. No change to the 24px value, the conformance level, or the square-fit definition. Not outdated.

4. CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE. Searched for disputes/criticism. Found none contesting the 24x24 AA figure or the square method. Adrian Roselli's widely used 24x24 Pixel Cursor Bookmarklet independently corroborates the square-fit test. Criticism in the field targets how the *spacing exception* is misunderstood, not the base requirement.

5. SOURCE QUALITY. Primary W3C/WAI normative Recommendation plus the official Understanding document. Matches or exceeds the claim's strength. Not marketing, not a press release, not forum speculation.

QUALIFICATIONS THE CLAIM UNDERSTATES (flagged, but not disqualifying):
(a) The claim states the 24x24 requirement unqualified. The SC has five exceptions, and the Spacing exception materially permits smaller targets: "Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target." So a 16x16 icon button can conform via spacing. The square-fit test is the measurement of size, not the sole path to conformance — a downstream write-up should carry the exceptions, especially Spacing and Inline.
(b) "not patch after build" is editorial framing not present in the source, and is technically loose — hit area can be enlarged post-build via CSS padding or a pseudo-element overlay without altering visual layout. The design-time framing is defensible for the research question but is the author's, not W3C's.

Neither disputes level, threshold, or measurement method.

REQUIRED QUALIFIER (incompleteness, not falsification): the claim states the flat 24x24 requirement and omits all five normative exceptions — Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential. The Spacing exception is materially load-bearing: "Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target". result.evidence:
Half the claim checks out; the load-bearing half is directly contradicted by the very source cited.

WHAT SURVIVES: the enumeration. The WCAG 2.2 glossary text on the cited page reads verbatim: "cognitive function test — A task that requires the user to remember, manipulate, or transcribe information. Examples include, but are not limited to: memorization, such as remembering a username, password, set of characters, images, or patterns...; transcription, such as typing in characters; use of correct spelling; performance of calculations; solving of puzzles." (The claim silently drops "use of correct spelling," and also drops the glossary's own carve-out: "The common identifiers name, e-mail, and phone number are not considered cognitive function tests as they are personal to the user and consistent across websites.")

WHAT IS REFUTED: the inference "a design that asks a user to read a one-time code on one device and retype it on another is a failing pattern absent an exception." The same Understanding page contains a paragraph written specifically to answer this question, and it says the opposite:

"There are scenarios where a verification code must be received or generated on a secondary device. For example, authenticating in a web browser on a laptop requires a verification code that is sent as an SMS text message to a mobile phone. However, in most cases, it is possible for the code to then be sent directly to the primary device... Evaluating whether or not the code can be seamlessly transferred from the secondary device to the primary device is outside of the scope for this success criterion. For the purpose of evaluating web content that relies on authentication using these types of secondary device systems, it is assumed that provisions are in place that make the code available in the user's clipboard. Evaluating this criterion therefore only requires verification that the web content does allow pasting the clipboard content in the related authentication challenge field."

So the cross-device read-and-retype scenario the claim names as "a failing pattern" is explicitly declared out of scope; conformance turns solely on whether the OTP field accepts a paste. The claim inverts the default. The actual normative failure is narrower — F109 "Failure of Success Criterion 3.3.8 and 3.3.9 due to preventing password or code re-entry in the same format" — i.e., blocking paste, blocking autofill, or splitting a 6-digit code across six one-character inputs (the page's Figure 3: "trying to paste the entire code only fills in one digit in the first input").

PROVENANCE OF THE CARVE-OUT: this is not an accident of drafting. w3c/wcag issue #2866 ("Accessible Authentication — one-time-passcodes and the test for when an activity requires 'transcription'") raised exactly the claim's reading, including the 30–60s TOTP window objection; it was closed by PR #3046, merged 2023-03-07, before WCAG 2.2 reached Recommendation (2023-10-05). The WG considered "cross-device OTP = fail" and declined to adopt it.

SECONDARY DEFECT: the supporting quote offered ("memorization, such as remembering a username, password, set of characters, images, or patterns") does not support the OTP conclusion at all — an OTP read off a screen is not memorized. The relevant example would be "transcription," and the page's transcription discussion is precisely where the out-of-scope carve-out lives. Quote and conclusion are mismatched.

The generous reading — "allowing paste is the Mechanism exception, so 'absent an exception' saves the claim" — still fails as design guidance: it tells a designer that ordinary SMS/TOTP-to-second-device auth is presumptively non-conforming and needs special justification, when W3C says such a design conforms as long as the input accepts a paste and does not fragment the field. For a research brief on what must be decided at design time, that is an actionable falsehood: the design decision 3.3.8 actually forces is "one pasteable/autofillable field, never per-character boxes, never a re-format challenge" — not "no cross-device OTP."

Both halves of the claim are confirmed verbatim in the cited primary source and its linked failure technique (fetched raw HTML, not just summaries).

PART 1 — copy/paste + password managers satisfy "Mechanism". This is stronger than the supplied quote: it is in the NORMATIVE SC text of 3.3.8, Note 2: "Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of re-typing." The mechanism definition on the same page explicitly permits reliance on the platform/user agent: "The mechanism may be explicitly provided in the content, or may be relied upon to be provided by either the platform or by user agents, including assistive technologies." So relying on the browser/3rd-party manager is legitimate, not an overreach.

PART 2 — blocking paste / re-entry in a different format is a failure. Understanding 3.3.8: "if user agents and password managers are actively blocked from filling in the fields (for instance, by a script that prevents form fields from being automatically populated), or users are prevented from copy and paste operations ... then the page would fail this criterion unless an alternative is provided." The page's Failures list cites F109 (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/failures/F109, "Updated 27 April 2026"), whose description reads: "Requiring users to authenticate by entering a password or code in a different format from which it was originally created is a failure to meet Success Criteria 3.3.8 ... and 3.3.9 ... result.evidence:
The first half of the claim checks out; the load-bearing second half is contradicted by the very page cited as its source.

WHAT IS CORRECT. The WCAG 2.2 glossary definition, reproduced verbatim in the Key Terms of the cited Understanding page, is: "cognitive function test — A task that requires the user to remember, manipulate, or transcribe information. Examples include, but are not limited to: memorization, such as remembering a username, password, set of characters, images, or patterns. The common identifiers name, e-mail, and phone number are not considered cognitive function tests as they are personal to the user and consistent across websites; transcription, such as typing in characters; use of correct spelling; performance of calculations; solving of puzzles." So the enumeration is real (the claim drops "use of correct spelling" and drops the name/email/phone carve-out, and calls it "concrete" when the list is expressly "not limited to" — minor, not fatal).

WHAT REFUTES IT. The same page has a section "Two-factor authentication systems (verification codes)" that addresses the exact scenario in the claim and reaches the opposite conclusion: "There are scenarios where a verification code must be received or generated on a secondary device. For example, authenticating in a web browser on a laptop requires a verification code that is sent as an SMS text message to a mobile phone. ... Evaluating whether or not the code can be seamlessly transferred from the secondary device to the primary device is outside of the scope for this success criterion. For the purpose of evaluating web content that relies on authentication using these types of secondary device systems, it is assumed that provisions are in place that make the code available in the user's clipboard. Evaluating this criterion therefore only requires verification that the web content does allow pasting the clipboard content in the related authentication challenge field."

That is a direct inversion of the claim's practical guidance. Cross-device OTP is not a "failing pattern absent an exception" — W3C explicitly declines to evaluate the cross-device hop at all and *assumes* clipboard availability. Conformance turns on exactly one testable thing: does the code field accept a paste (and allow user-agent autofill). A designer shipping SMS-to-phone → enter-on-laptop with one paste-friendly input conforms. The actual failing patterns the page names are narrower and different: blocking paste into auth fields (Figure 2), splitting the 6-digit code into six one-digit inputs so a paste only fills the first box (Figure 3), and format-mismatch prompts like "enter the 1st, 3rd and 5th character of your password" (Figure 4). The claim's version would send a designer to remove a pattern W3C permits while missing the segmented-input failure W3C actually flags.

OUTDATED / DISPUTED. This exact question was litigated in the WG: w3c/wcag issue #2866, "Accessible Authentication - one-time-passcodes and the test for when an activity requires 'transcription'", raised because the Understanding text only mentioned copying from a "local source" and said nothing about cross-device. It was closed by PR #3046 (merged 2023-03-07, before WCAG 2.2 reached Recommendation on 2023-10-05), and the "outside of the scope … assumed provisions are in place" paragraph is that PR's resolution. The claim reproduces the pre-clarification reading the WG explicitly walked back.

QUOTE-vs-CLAIM GAP. The supplied supporting quote ("memorization, such as remembering a username, password, set of characters, images, or patterns") supports only the memorization bullet. It carries no weight for the transcription/calculation/puzzle items and none at all for the OTP conclusion — which is the part the source refutes.

Split verdict: the enumeration half checks out verbatim; the load-bearing inference about cross-device OTPs is contradicted by the SAME primary page.

WHAT IS SUPPORTED. The WCAG 2.2 glossary (quoted in Understanding 3.3.8, https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html) reads: "A task that requires the user to remember, manipulate, or transcribe information. Examples include, but are not limited to: memorization, such as remembering a username, password, set of characters, images, or patterns... transcription, such as typing in characters; use of correct spelling; performance of calculations; solving of puzzles." So memorization/transcription/calculation/puzzles are genuinely listed.

WHY THE CLAIM STILL FAILS.
(1) "Enumerated concretely" misreads an explicitly OPEN list — the spec says "include, but are not limited to." The claim also drops two designer-relevant items from the same definition: "use of correct spelling," and the carve-out that "The common identifiers name, e-mail, and phone number are NOT considered cognitive function tests as they are personal to the user and consistent across websites."
(2) "Prohibited" is wrong. SC 3.3.8 (AA, W3C Recommendation 12 Dec 2024) permits a cognitive function test whenever the step provides Alternative, Mechanism, Object Recognition, or Personal Content. Nothing is categorically prohibited.
(3) The OTP conclusion is directly contradicted. The same Understanding page addresses the exact scenario the claim describes — a code on a phone, entered on a laptop — and declines to fail it: "There are scenarios where a verification code must be received or generated on a secondary device. For example, authenticating in a web browser on a laptop requires a verification code that is sent as an SMS text message to a mobile phone... Evaluating whether or not the code can be seamlessly transferred from the secondary device to the primary device is outside of the scope for this success criterion. For the purpose of evaluating web content that relies on authentication using these types of secondary device systems, it is ASSUMED that provisions are in place that make the code available in the user's clipboard. Evaluating this criterion therefore only requires verification that the web content does allow pasting the clipboard content in the related authentication challenge field." That inverts the claim's burden: W3C presumes the cross-device flow passes and tests only paste-allowance. The registered failure technique is F109, "Failure of Success Criterion 3.3.8 and 3.3.9 due to preventing password or code re-entry in the same format" — i.e. the failure is BLOCKING paste/autofill, not the read-it-here-type-it-there UX.
(4) The claim's hedge "absent an exception" does not rescue it: the escape here is not one of the SC's four listed exceptions, it is a scoping assumption plus "Copy and paste can be relied on to avoid transcription" (no cognitive function test arises at all). A designer following the claim literally would conclude SMS/authenticator 2FA must be dropped to conform, which the primary source explicitly does not say.

The defensible restatement, and the only sentence the source supports, is the narrower one on the same page: "A service that requires MANUAL transcription of a verification code is not compliant... it must be possible for a user to at least paste the code... and to allow user agents to fill in the fields automatically." Design rule = never block paste or autofill in an OTP/password field; not "cross-device OTP is a failing pattern."

Source quality is fine (W3C primary, current — Rec 12 Dec 2024, no relevant erratum found); the defect is misreading, not staleness or marketing.

HALF 1 (password managers / paste satisfy "Mechanism") — supported by the SC's own NORMATIVE Note 2, which is stronger than the informative quote the claim cited: "Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of re-typing." (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html). Understanding adds the design-time dependency: fields must meet 1.3.5 Input Purpose and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value so "user agents and password managers should be able to reliably recognize the fields and automatically fill them in."

HALF 2 (blocking paste / format change = failure) — supported by a dedicated failure technique, F109 "Failure of Success Criterion 3.3.8 and 3.3.9 due to preventing password or code re-entry in the same format" (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/failures/F109). Understanding: "if user agents and password managers are actively blocked from filling in the fields ... or users are prevented from copy and paste operations ... then the page would fail this criterion unless an alternative is provided." And: "using a different format between the copied text and the input field (for example, 'Enter the 1st, 3rd, and 5th character of your password') would force the user to transcribe information and therefore fail this criterion, unless another method is available."

TWO QUALIFICATIONS the claim omits and that the parent write-up MUST carry, or it will mislead designers:

(a) The failure is CONDITIONAL, not absolute. F109 Description: "...is a failure to meet Success Criteria 3.3.8 and 3.3.9 (unless alternative authentication methods are available)." F109's test procedure is explicitly two-step — expected result: "If both checks #1 and #2 are false, then this failure condition applies." So a site offering a passkey/biometric/magic-link Alternative can block paste and still pass. The claim's flat "is a failure of the criterion" overstates this. The four routes (Alternative, Mechanism, Object Recognition, Personal Content) are independent — meeting any one suffices.

(b) Split OTP digit boxes are not automatically a failure. F109 lists as a failure "a fieldset that prompts a user to enter each digit of a verification code in a separate input" — but with the carve-out "(unless the user can paste the entire code in the first input, and the remaining inputs are populated automatically)." That is a concrete design-time decision worth stating.

Also noted, not refuting: w3c/wcag issue #1855 shows community confusion about conflating "user can paste from a third-party manager" with "works with password managers" — these are two distinct mechanisms, and only the first is what the cited quote covers. Currency: SC 3.3.8 text and F109 as served today are unchanged; WCAG 2.2 has been a W3C Recommendation since Oct 2023 (2nd ed. Dec 2024) and the errata affected 4.1.1 Parsing, not 3.3.8.

1) Normative text, https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ (the Recommendation itself, not just Understanding):

That is a direct, verbatim confirmation of the claim's "partial obscuring passes at AA" — it is not an inference or overreach from the quoted SC text.

Adversarial checks run and failed to refute:
- Searched for dispute/qualification. Independent secondary sources (TPGi/Vispero, Silktide, DigitalA11Y, Stark) all state the same reading: partial obscuring does not fail 2.4.11 but does fail 2.4.12. The only "criticism" found is a POLICY complaint (2.4.11's threshold is weak because even mostly-covered elements pass), which reinforces rather than contradicts the claim's factual content.

Caveats that qualify but do not refute: the Understanding doc adds scope conditions the claim does not mention — only the INITIAL position of user-movable content is tested; content the user opened that can be revealed/dismissed without advancing focus is not counted as hiding the component; properly constructed modals pass because they take focus. One trivial wording drift: 2.4.12's normative verb is "hidden by," while the claim paraphrases as "obscured" — the SC's own title uses "Obscured," so this is synonymous, not a misread.

result.evidence:
Claim holds against primary W3C sources; I tried three refutation angles and none landed.

1) Quote-support check — the claim is NOT an overreach of its quote, and additional verbatim text from the same page backs both halves:
- Mechanism exception, SC 3.3.8 Note 2 (w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html): "support for password entry by password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of re-typing." The normative Mechanism bullet is generic ("A mechanism is available to assist the user in completing the cognitive function test"), and the Note is what attributes password managers / copy-paste to it — so the claim's attribution is correct, just sourced from the Note rather than the bullet.
- Failure half, same page: "if user agents and password managers are actively blocked from filling in the fields (for instance, by a script that prevents form fields from being automatically populated), or users are prevented from copy and paste operations (as they may rely on standalone/external third party password managers), then the page would fail this criterion unless an alternative is provided."
- The page also states the design requirement for codes: "it must be possible for a user to at least paste the code (such as from a standalone third-party password manager, text message application, or software-based security key), and to allow user agents to fill in the fields automatically."

2) The claim's "same format" wording is near-verbatim W3C, not the reviewer's paraphrase. F109 (w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/failures/F109) is titled "Failure of Success Criterion 3.3.8 and 3.3.9 due to preventing password or code re-entry in the same format" and its Description reads: "Requiring users to authenticate by entering a password or code in a different format from which it was originally created is a failure to meet Success Criteria 3.3.8 and 3.3.9 (unless alternative authentication methods are available)." Failure examples include per-character fieldsets ("Enter the 2nd, 6th and last characters of your password"), one-input-per-digit OTP fields "(unless the user can paste the entire code in the first input, and the remaining inputs are populated automatically)", and <select>-based password entry.

3) Contradiction search: the only substantive dispute I found is w3c/wcag issue #1855, which argued the Understanding doc conflates password-manager DOM injection (which does not fire a `paste` event) with manual CTRL+V. That issue was CLOSED and resolved via PR #1898 — and the currently published Understanding text already reflects the fix by listing the two blocking mechanisms disjunctively ("blocked from filling in the fields ... or ... prevented from copy and paste"). So the dispute refined the wording rather than refuting the claim. Independent corroboration: NIST SP 800-63B tells verifiers to permit paste to facilitate password managers.

Currency: WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation (Oct 2023, updated Dec 2024) and 3.3.8 is unchanged; F109 is live at the WCAG 2.2 Techniques URL. Not marketing, not forum speculation — primary W3C normative + supporting-technique documents.

One qualification a designer-facing brief should carry (imprecision, not refutation): the claim states the failure unconditionally, while both W3C texts hedge it — "unless an alternative is provided" (Understanding) / "unless alternative authentication methods are available" (F109). F109's Expected Results makes this a two-part test: "If both checks #1 and #2 are false, then this failure condition applies" — i.e. (1) field does not allow entry in the original format AND (2) no alternative accessible authentication exists. Blocking paste while offering a genuinely non-cognitive alternative (e.g. WebAuthn/passkey, email magic link) still passes.
