Claim confirmed on all three assertions (level, "entirely hidden" threshold, AAA sibling) against the normative primary source, with no contradicting evidence found.

1) LEVEL + NORMATIVE TEXT — W3C WCAG 2.2 Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/, current version dated 12 December 2024): SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) is **Level AA**, text verbatim: "When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content." SC 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) is **Level AAA**: "When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, no part of the component is hidden by author-created content." Both the level assignments and the "entirely hidden" vs "no part" contrast in the claim match the normative text exactly.

2) PARTIAL-OBSCURING READING IS NOT AN OVERREACH — this is the checklist's main risk (inferring "partial passes" from a bare quote), but the Understanding doc states it explicitly rather than leaving it to inference: "this AA criterion allows for the component receiving focus to be *partially* obscured by other author-created content," and "For best visibility, *none* of the component receiving focus should be obscured. This preferred outcome is covered by the AAA criterion Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)." So the claim's supporting quote under-sells its own support; the source says the claim's exact proposition in its own words.

3) ADVERSARIAL CHECK ON THE NOTES — I checked whether the two Notes attached to 2.4.11 tighten the requirement beyond "not entirely hidden" (which would qualify the claim). They do the opposite; both RELAX it. Note 1: "Where content in a configurable interface can be repositioned by the user, then only the initial positions of user-movable content are considered for testing and conformance of this success criterion." Note 2: "Content opened by the user may obscure the component receiving focus. If the user can reveal the focused component without advancing the keyboard focus, the component with focus is not considered visually hidden due to author-created content." No note makes the criterion stricter, so nothing undercuts "partial obscuring passes at AA."

4) INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION — TPGi/Vispero (independent accessibility testing authority) test guidance corroborates: partially obscuring an element does not fail 2.4.11 although it would fail SC 2.4.12 at AAA, which requires no part of the control be obscured under the same circumstances. Search for disputes/heavy qualifications of this reading returned none; every secondary source located (TPGi, Silktide, Appt, AAArdvark, DigitalA11Y, HK Digital Policy Office) agrees, and several note the only common error is the reverse misconception (people wrongly assuming AA forbids partial obscuring).

5) SOURCE QUALITY / CURRENCY — primary W3C normative REC plus the official Understanding document; source strength exceeds what this modest, non-extraordinary claim requires. Not marketing, not a press release, not forum speculation. Currency verified: WCAG 2.2 as amended 12 Dec 2024 is the operative version as of July 2026 (the Dec 2024 amendment removed SC 4.1.1 Parsing; it did not alter 2.4.11 or 2.4.12).

ONLY IMPRECISION FOUND (non-material, does not warrant refutation): the normative text of 2.4.12 uses the word "hidden" while the SC *title* uses "obscured"; the claim uses "obscured" for both. The claim also omits the "by author-created content" qualifier in its AAA half, though the first clause carries it by context. Neither alters the substance of any of the three assertions.
result.counterSource: No credible counter-source located. Targeted search for disputes/qualifications of the "partial obscuring passes at AA" reading surfaced only agreement (TPGi https://www.tpgi.com/how-to-test-2-4-11-focus-not-obscured-minimum/, Silktide, Appt, AAArdvark, DigitalA11Y, HK Digital Policy Office). The strongest available counter-angle — that the two Notes on 2.4.11 might impose stricter conditions than "not entirely hidden" — was checked directly against the Understanding doc and failed: both Notes relax the criterion (initial-position-only testing for user-movable content; user-opened content exempt when the user can reveal the focused component without advancing focus).

result.evidence:
Verified verbatim against the primary source (fetched 2026-07-28; the W3C Understanding page shows "Last Updated: 15 June 2026"). The Intent section of https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-not-obscured-minimum.html contains exactly: "Typical types of content that can overlap focused items are sticky footers, sticky headers, and non-modal dialogs." So the enumeration in the claim is not a paraphrase or a misread — it is the source's own list, in the source's own order.

The design-time gloss is also supported rather than invented. The same Understanding doc's Intent opens "The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that the item receiving keyboard focus is always partially visible in the user's viewport," and its remedies are all layout/composition decisions, not post-build code fixes: use CSS scroll-padding to offset focus from the sticky block; make additional content reflow the main content area instead of overlapping it ("no overlapping content between sections so the focused item will not be obscured"); make the content modal; or auto-dismiss on focus loss. Choosing reflow-vs-overlay is a concept-stage layout decision, which is what the claim asserts.

Attempted refutations, and why they fail to kill it:
1. Normative vs non-normative. Real but minor imprecision. The claim says "the criterion targets… are named," yet the three examples appear ONLY in the non-normative Understanding/Intent prose. The normative SC 2.4.11 text (checked at https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) is generic: "When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content." 2.4.12 Enhanced: "…no part of the component is hidden by author-created content." The claim cites the Understanding page as its source and quotes it accurately, so this is an attribution nuance, not a false statement. Downstream use should say "the Understanding document names…" rather than "the criterion names…".
2. Notes that qualify scope. SC 2.4.11 Note 1 (only initial positions of user-repositionable content are tested) and Note 2 ("Content opened by the user may obscure the component receiving focus. If the user can reveal the focused component without advancing the keyboard focus, the component with focus is not considered visually hidden…") mean a user-opened non-modal dialog can pass without the author changing the layout. These qualify conformance testing; they do not contradict the claim that author-placed persistent overlays are the named typical offenders. Note also 2.4.11 is only "not entirely hidden" — a sticky header that partially covers focus passes AA and fails AAA 2.4.12. The claim does not overstate this (it does not say sticky = failure).
3. Contradicting sources. None found. Search returned only secondary explainers (TestParty 2025 guide, AllAccessible, AccessiTREE, tabnav, wcag.dock.codes) that all restate the same three content types plus the scroll-padding/reflow design remedies; W3C failure technique F110 covers the same ground. No credible dispute, no marketing/benchmark/forum basis, nothing outdated — WCAG 2.2 has been a W3C Recommendation since Oct 2023 and the cited page is current as of June 2026.
result.counterSource: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ — normative SC 2.4.11/2.4.12 text names no content types (only "author-created content"), and Notes 1–2 exempt user-repositionable and user-opened content under conditions; the three examples exist only in the non-normative Understanding prose, so "the criterion … are named" should be reworded to "the Understanding document names".

result.evidence: Tried to refute; the core survives. Verbatim check against the cited primary source (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-not-obscured-minimum.html, Intent section) confirms the quote word-for-word: "A notification implemented as sticky content, such as a cookie banner, will fail this success criterion if it entirely obscures a component receiving focus. Ways of passing include making the banner modal so the user has to dismiss the banner before navigating through the page, or using scroll padding so the banner does not overlap other content." Both designs are corroborated elsewhere on the same page's Examples section: a sticky-footer example passing via scroll padding, and "A page has a full-width cookie approval dialog. The dialog is modal, preventing access to the other controls in the page until it has been dismissed." The scroll-padding route is further backed by a formal W3C sufficient technique, C43 "Using CSS scroll-padding to un-obscure content" (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/css/C43.html), whose worked example is literally a fixed-position bottom banner of the cookie-consent kind. Source quality is primary W3C for a modest descriptive claim; not marketing, not forum speculation. Currency: WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation and this Understanding text is live as of this check (2026-07); no contradicting source found — searches surfaced only qualifications, not disputes. Two caveats that qualify without refuting: (1) paraphrase drift — W3C says the modal must be dismissed "before navigating through the page" (i.e. moving keyboard focus through page content), whereas the claim's "before page navigation" can be misread as navigating away to another page; the underlying design decision (modal blocks access to other controls until dismissed) is nonetheless exactly what W3C states. (2) The scroll-padding route carries known implementation limits that the claim's flat "never overlaps" wording hides — w3c/wcag issue #3532 notes C43 as written is sufficient only for 2.4.11 AA, not 2.4.12 AAA; TPGI and TetraLogical document that scroll-padding is not triggered by JAWS virtual-cursor navigation, needs dynamic recalculation when header height changes (e.g. user font-size), and needs a media query so it does not apply when the header is not sticky. Also note "Ways of passing include" is non-exhaustive, so "two concrete passing designs" is accurate as examples, not as the only options. The "decided at design time" framing is the researcher's, not W3C's, though modal-vs-inline banner is genuinely a concept-stage decision.

TWO DRIFTS TO CORRECT IN THE WRITE-UP, neither fatal: (1) the claim's "dismissed before page navigation" mis-compresses W3C's "before navigating through the page", which means keyboard traversal WITHIN the page, not navigating away to another page — the claim's phrasing invites building a navigation-blocking cookie wall, a different and GDPR-fraught design; (2) W3C says "Ways of passing INCLUDE", explicitly non-exhaustive, and the same sentence pair names a third way ("Notifications that do not require user action could also meet this criterion by closing on loss of focus"), so "names two" must not be presented as the complete set. Attempted refutation on all five checklist axes; claim survived each.

(1) Quote supports claim — verified verbatim at the primary source. WebFetch of https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/ returns document status "W3C Working Draft, published March 3, 2026" and confirms the sentence "While this draft has moved closer towards completion, it still has several years of work." Both factual assertions (WD status; date 3 March 2026; WG's own several-years statement) are directly attested by the cited primary source, not paraphrased.

(2) The inferential leap ("no 2026 design or procurement decision can be anchored to WCAG 3 conformance") is the only part not literally in the quote — but it is independently supported by (a) W3C's own status boilerplate on the same page: "This is a draft document and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any time. It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress" and "Publication as a Working Draft does not imply endorsement by W3C and its Members"; and (b) the fact that WCAG 3's conformance model itself (Bronze/Silver/Gold, process assertions) is explicitly still under public review in the March 2026 draft with unfilled specification tables — you cannot claim conformance to a conformance model that is not finalized. So the inference is not an overreach.

(3) Searched for contradicting evidence; none found. Every actual legal instrument in force references WCAG 2.x, never WCAG 3: DOJ ADA Title II final rule requires WCAG 2.1 Level AA (DOJ Interim Final Rule of 17 April 2026 extended deadlines to 26 April 2027 for large public entities and 26 April 2028 for smaller entities/special districts — an extension of the WCAG 2.1 obligation, with no substitution of WCAG 3); EN 301 549 V3.2.1 incorporates WCAG 2.1 in full, and the forthcoming v4.1.1 (2026) moves to WCAG 2.2 AA — still not WCAG 3; Section 508 likewise sits on WCAG 2.x. This is corroborating, not contradicting, evidence for the procurement half of the claim.

(4) Not outdated. Checked for a post-March supersession: w3.org publication history and W3C 2026 news show no WCAG 3 Working Draft published in April–July 2026. The 3 March 2026 draft (and its companion DNOTE-wcag-3.0-explainer-20260303) remains the current publication as of today, 28 July 2026. Secondary trackers put Candidate Recommendation around Q4 2027 and Recommendation no earlier than 2028 — consistent with "several years of work," and if anything more conservative than the claim.

(5) Not marketing/press-release/forum material. Source is w3.org/TR — the normative primary source, published by the group that authors the specification. Source quality exceeds what the claim's strength requires; the claim is a modest, verifiable status statement rather than an extraordinary one.

Only quibble, insufficient to refute: the claim's absolute phrasing "no ... can be anchored" is rhetorically strong, but it is accurate in the strict sense that no conformance claim against WCAG 3 is definable today, and W3C itself forbids citing the document as anything but work in progress.
result.counterSource: No credible counter-source located. The quote is not truncated or reframed; the claim restates exactly what it says.

The second clause ("no 2026 design or procurement decision can be anchored to WCAG 3 conformance") goes beyond the supplied quote, so I checked whether it is independently supported. It is, from the same primary document: Status of This Document also carries "It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress" and "This is a draft document and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any time"; the draft states "The final set of requirements in WCAG 3 will be different from what is in this draft. Requirements are likely to be added, combined, and removed"; and the conformance section is explicitly NOT finalized — the WG is still soliciting feedback on the conformance model structure itself. There is literally no stable conformance model to anchor to. Corroborated by W3C WAI's own overview page (https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/wcag3-intro/, last updated 3 March 2026): "Many aspects of W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3 are in an exploratory or developing phase and will change substantially" and "WCAG 3 is not expected to be a completed W3C standard for a few more years."

(3) OUTDATED? No. Today is 2026-07-28; 3 March 2026 is still the latest published Working Draft. Searched W3C news for June/July 2026 WCAG 3 publications — none found. The only newer artifact is the rolling Editor's Draft at w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/, which is by definition even less citable than a WD and does not change the claim.

(4) CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE / REGULATORY CROSS-CHECK. No credible source disputes it. On the procurement half specifically: no jurisdiction references WCAG 3 — Section 508 keys to WCAG 2.0 AA, the DOJ ADA Title II rule to WCAG 2.1 AA, and the EAA via EN 301 549 to WCAG 2.1 AA with v4.1.1 (2026) moving to WCAG 2.2 AA. The regulatory direction of travel in 2026 is 2.1 → 2.2, not toward 3.0.

(5) SOURCE QUALITY. Primary W3C TR + primary W3C WAI, which matches or exceeds the claim's strength. Not marketing, not a press release, not forum speculation.

CAVEATS (do not refute, but should be carried forward): (a) The claim is correctly silent on dates. Widely circulated figures of "Candidate Recommendation Q4 2027 / Recommendation not before 2028" come only from secondary vendor blogs, NOT from W3C — do not attribute those dates to a primary source. W3C WAI states only that the WG "plans to develop a projected WCAG 3 timeline by April 2026"; I found no published W3C timeline document. (b) "Can be anchored" is strictly true for conformance, but a team may still voluntarily read WCAG 3 drafts as directional design guidance (e.g. APCA-style contrast thinking) — that is not conformance and should not be presented as such.

1. QUOTE VERIFIED VERBATIM. Fetched the live canonical https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/ (a /TR/ URL always serves the latest published version, so this is current as of 2026-07-28). It returns a W3C Working Draft dated 03 March 2026 containing, word for word: "WCAG 2 is used around the world and will still be required by different countries for a long time to come." Adjacent text: "WCAG 3 is a successor to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2 but does not deprecate WCAG 2." Not a paraphrase, not cherry-picked.

2. INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED ON A SECOND W3C PROPERTY. w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/wcag3-intro/ (last updated 3 March 2026): "WCAG 3 will not supersede WCAG 2 and WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for at least several years after WCAG 3 is finalized." Two independent W3C pages, same position. The claim's "will not replace" is exactly W3C's "does not deprecate" / "will not supersede."

3. NOT OUTDATED. March 2026 draft is the newest; today is 28 Jul 2026. The draft self-describes: "While this draft has moved closer towards completion, it still has several years of work. Details will change." Third-party trackers put Candidate Recommendation at ~Q4 2027 and Recommendation not before 2028. Nothing suggests W3C reversed course.

4. THE ONE UNQUOTED INFERENCE HOLDS INDEPENDENTLY. "WCAG 2.2 is the operative design-time target" is not in the quote, so I attacked it directly — most laws name 2.1 or 2.0, not 2.2. But w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/ defeats the attack: "W3C encourages you to use the latest version of WCAG" and "Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 also conforms to WCAG 2.1 and WCAG 2.0" plus "If you want to meet all the versions, you can use the WCAG 2.2 resources and you do not need to look at earlier versions." WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation (5 Oct 2023, updated 12 Dec 2024, now ISO/IEC 40500:2025) and is a backward-compatible superset, so designing to 2.2 satisfies every version any current law names. The inference is strengthened, not weakened, by the version audit.

5. SOURCE QUALITY MATCHES CLAIM STRENGTH. Primary W3C normative-track document plus primary WAI explainer. Not marketing, not a press release, not a vendor blog, not forum speculation.

PRECISION NOTE for the parent (does not refute): the claim's phrase "legally required standard" is slightly stronger than W3C's wording — W3C says "required by different countries," never uses "legally." Substantively equivalent (country-level requirement = regulatory), but the write-up should not put "legally" inside quotation marks as W3C's words. Separately, the write-up should not imply the string "WCAG 2.2" appears in current US statutes/regulations — it does not; 2.2 is the correct design target because it is a superset of the versions that are cited.

VERIFIED AGAINST LIVE PRIMARY SOURCE. Fetched https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/ (W3C Working Draft, dated 03 March 2026 — current, not stale). The supporting quote is present VERBATIM in the live document, in §1.2 "About WCAG 3": "Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 Level A and Level AA is expected to meet most of the minimum conformance level of this new standard but, since WCAG 3 includes additional tests and different scoring mechanics, additional work will be needed to reach full conformance."

(1) Quote supports claim, no overreach. The claim is a near-verbatim restatement. It preserves the W3C's own hedge ("expected to"), and "most, but not all" is a fair reading of "most ... additional work will be needed to reach full conformance." The claim adds no causal or predictive weight the source doesn't carry.

(2) Searched for contradiction; found none. Secondary sources (AbilityNet, Vispero, AFixt, accessibility.build) all agree in the same direction: the minimum/Bronze level = meeting all Foundational Requirements, "designed to be roughly comparable to WCAG 2.2 AA" — roughly, not identically. The W3C Explainer (https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/DNOTE-wcag-3.0-explainer-20260226/) is consistent: "It does not deprecate WCAG 2" and "WCAG 3 will not be published until it covers at least as much as WCAG 2.2" — parity of scope, not automatic carry-over of conformance. Nothing disputes the claim.

(3) Source quality matches claim strength. Primary W3C TR document; the claim is modest and hedged, so a Working Draft is adequate support for a statement about what WCAG 3 currently proposes.

(4) Not outdated — 03 March 2026 draft, four months old at time of check.

(5) Not marketing/forum speculation — W3C normative-track document.

CAVEATS the parent should carry forward (qualifications, not refutations): (a) the source self-labels as unstable — "This is a draft document and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any time. It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress," and §3 Conformance carries an editor's note that "the conformance model has been updated, there are several questions in the conformance section." (b) The March 2026 Conformance section does not itself name levels (it says only "several levels of conformance are available") nor spell out the scoring, so the intro's phrase "different scoring mechanics" currently outruns the draft's own normative text — Bronze/Silver/Gold naming comes from secondary commentary and prior drafts, not the current §3. (c) Timeline is genuinely unsettled: the Explainer gives no Recommendation date, notes the WG was "currently chartered through April 2026," and secondary sources put a final standard no earlier than 2028. So the claim should be attributed as "W3C's current stated expectation," not as a settled fact about a shipping standard.
result.counterSource: No contradicting source found. Strongest qualifier is the draft's own status warning and the §3 editor's note flagging open conformance questions (https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/), plus the Explainer's silence on carry-over of 2.2 conformance (https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/DNOTE-wcag-3.0-explainer-20260226/).

result.evidence: Tried to refute; could not. (1) Quote is verbatim and current. Fetched https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/ raw (741KB HTML, stripped tags) — masthead reads "W3C Working Draft 03 March 2026" (this version: /TR/2026/WD-wcag-3.0-20260303/). The Introduction's plain-language summary contains, word for word: "WCAG 3 is a newer standard than the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2. WCAG 3 does not replace WCAG 2. WCAG 2 is used around the world and will still be required by different countries for a long time to come. Meeting WCAG 2 at AA level means you will be close to meeting WCAG 3, but there may be differences." The normative Introduction independently says: "WCAG 3 is a successor to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2 [WCAG22] and previous versions, but does not deprecate WCAG 2." (2) Timeline corroborates operativeness: same document's status section — "While this draft has moved closer towards completion, it still has several years of work"; "Publication as a Working Draft does not imply endorsement... It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress." W3C WAI's WCAG 3 Introduction (last updated 3 March 2026) adds: "WCAG 3 will not supersede WCAG 2 and WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for at least several years after WCAG 3 is finalized" and "WCAG 3 is not expected to be a completed W3C standard for a few more years." (3) The inference "WCAG 2.2 is the operative design-time target" is separately supported by a primary source — https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/ states "W3C encourages you to use the latest version of WCAG" and "WCAG 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2 are designed to be 'backwards compatible', which means content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 also conforms to WCAG 2.1 and WCAG 2.0. If you want to meet all the versions, you can use the WCAG 2.2 resources and you do not need to look at earlier versions." Same page: WCAG 2.2 is now ISO/IEC 40500:2025, and "EN 301 549 currently uses WCAG 2.1. We expect the next version of EN 301 549 to use the latest version of WCAG 2.2." No credible source disputes any part; searches surfaced only agreeing secondary coverage (Deque, Level Access, W3C WAI Current Work). Source is the primary W3C TR itself, matching the claim's strength; not marketing, not outdated (March 2026 draft, checked July 2026).
result.counterSource: Two qualifications found, neither refuting: (a) the quoted sentence lives in the informative "Plain language summary of Introduction" — non-normative — though the normative Introduction says the same thing in stronger terms ("does not deprecate WCAG 2"); (b) W3C's wording is "required by different countries", not the claim's "legally required standard", and the versions actually cited in law today are older than 2.2 — EN 301 549 v3.2.1 references WCAG 2.1 AA (per w3.org/WAI: "EN 301 549 currently uses WCAG 2.1"), the DOJ ADA Title II rule adopts WCAG 2.1 AA, and Section 508 references WCAG 2.0 AA. So "WCAG 2.2" is the design-time target by W3C's own advice and backwards-compatibility, not because any statute names 2.2 — a designer targeting 2.2 conforms to 2.1/2.0 by construction, so the practical conclusion stands.

result.evidence: Tried to refute; could not. (1) QUOTE IS REAL AND EXACT: WebFetch of https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/ returns the sentence verbatim: "Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 Level A and Level AA is expected to meet most of the minimum conformance level of this new standard but, since WCAG 3 includes additional tests and different scoring mechanics, additional work will be needed to reach full conformance." Independently reproduced via a second w3.org-restricted search. (2) NO OVERREACH: claim's "most, but not all" = "expected to meet most of"; "will still require additional work later" = "additional work will be needed to reach full conformance"; the claim preserves the source's "is expected to" hedge. It is a restatement, not an inference. (3) CURRENT: document dated 03 March 2026 (~4 months old), the newest WCAG 3 WD, confirmed against W3C publication history and the WAI news item "For Review: WCAG 3 Working Draft - March 2026". (4) SOURCE QUALITY MATCHES: primary W3C TR for a modest forward-looking expectation. (5) ADVERSARIAL SEARCH FOUND QUALIFICATION, NOT CONTRADICTION: critics (Eric Eggert "WCAG 3 is not ready yet", Adrian Roselli "WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026") attack readiness/timeline, which cuts TOWARD the claim - more instability means more future work. The only near-contradiction located is the reverse-direction point (WCAG 3-conformant pages won't necessarily conform to WCAG 2.2), which the claim does not assert. Report the claim with the draft-status caveat attached. Also note for accuracy: the TR itself does not name the levels; the March 2026 explainer names Bronze (minimum)/Silver/Gold.
result.counterSource: No refuting source found. Nearest challenges are qualifications that support the claim's direction: Eric Eggert, "WCAG 3 is not ready yet - And it won't be for quite some time" (yatil.net) and Adrian Roselli, "WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026" (adrianroselli.com) both argue the conformance model is unstable; W3C's own WAI intro (https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/wcag3-intro/) states aspects "will change substantially" and the conformance model needs "the next few years" of work - which qualifies the certainty of the mechanism but reinforces that additional work will be required.

result.evidence:
ATTEMPTED REFUTATION FAILED — the claim survives on all five checklist axes.

1. QUOTE VERIFIED VERBATIM, INDEPENDENTLY. I did not rely on WebFetch (my first call was contaminated — I had pasted the quote into the prompt, inviting confirmation bias). I curled the raw document (741,587 bytes), stripped tags, and string-matched. The sentence exists character-for-character in the live W3C Working Draft: "Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 Level A and Level AA is expected to meet most of the minimum conformance level of this new standard but, since WCAG 3 includes additional tests and different scoring mechanics, additional work will be needed to reach full conformance." Located at §1.2 "About WCAG 3". Document masthead: "Working Draft 03 March 2026" — the current draft, 4 months old, not stale.

2. NOT AN OVERREACH. The claim's paraphrase "most, but not all" is a fair reading of "meet most of the minimum conformance level ... additional work will be needed to reach full conformance." The claim's terminology also checks out against the normative text: §3.2.1 literally defines "Bronze conformance (the minimum level of conformance)", so "WCAG 3's minimum conformance level" is the draft's own current term, not an invention. Even the claim's strong verb ("will still require additional work") mirrors W3C's own "will be needed."

3. NO CONTRADICTING SOURCE FOUND. Adversarial searches for criticism/dispute returned only corroboration or unrelated criticism. Eric Eggert's critical post (yatil.net, "WCAG 3 is not ready yet") attacks readiness and timeline, not this proposition. Secondary sources (AbilityNet, Vispero) restate the same point — "isn't backwards compatible with WCAG 2.x ... additional tests and different scoring mechanisms."

4. SOURCE QUALITY EXCEEDS CLAIM STRENGTH. Primary W3C TR document; claim is modestly hedged ("expected to"), matching the source's own hedge.

THREE QUALIFICATIONS the research output should carry, none of which refute the claim:
(a) STATUS: The quote sits in an informative introduction, not a normative section, of a document whose Status of This Document says: "This is a draft document and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any time. It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress." The conformance threshold is literally unfinished — §3.2.1 requires "some portion (to be determined) of the supplemental requirements."
(b) "SCORING MECHANICS" IS LIKELY VESTIGIAL. I counted occurrences across the whole document: "scoring" appears exactly ONCE — inside this very sentence. "score" = 0, "percent" = 0. No scoring model is described anywhere in the current conformance section; §3.2.1 is requirement-satisfaction-based (Bronze/Silver/Gold = all core requirements + increasing portions of supplemental requirements/assertions). The percentage/points scoring of earlier WCAG 3 drafts appears to have been dropped while this intro sentence was not updated. The claim faithfully reports the source; the staleness is the source's, not the claim's.
(c) "LATER" IS CONDITIONAL, NOT INEVITABLE. The immediately following sentence in the same paragraph: "the Accessibility Guidelines Working Group expects that some organizations may wish to continue using WCAG 2, while others may wish to migrate to the new standard. For those that wish to migrate to WCAG 3, the Working Group will provide transition support materials, which may use mapping and other approaches to facilitate migration." Additional work is required only if an org migrates. No regulation (EN 301 549, Section 508, DOJ Title II) references WCAG 3; Recommendation is projected 2028 at the earliest, with AGWG co-chair Rachael Bradley Montgomery publicly targeting end of 2029.

result.summary: The verified body of evidence covers only the first two of the eight requested areas — WCAG 2.2's new success criteria and WCAG 3.0's status — but covers them at normative-text depth from W3C primary sources. The design-time answer for WCAG 2.2 is concrete: six of the nine new criteria land at Level A/AA and each converts a formerly-implicit design decision into a measurable spec item — a 24x24 CSS px effective target area (2.5.8 AA), a visible non-drag affordance for every author-built drag interaction (2.5.7 AA), layout geometry or scroll-padding that keeps focused elements from being entirely covered by sticky chrome (2.4.11 AA), an authentication flow that never requires an unaided cognitive function test and never blocks paste or password managers (3.3.8 AA), re-use of previously entered data within a process (3.3.7 A), and consistently-placed help (3.2.6 A). WCAG 3.0 is a Working Draft dated 3 March 2026 whose own text says it "still has several years of work" and explicitly does not deprecate WCAG 2, so WCAG 2.2 AA is the operative 2026 design target while the binding legal instruments still name WCAG 2.1 (EU/DOJ) or 2.0 (Section 508). Areas 3 through 8 of the brief — ARIA APG patterns, SPA focus management, live regions, accessible names, the legal-enforcement detail, and native iOS/Android — produced no claims that survived verification and must be treated as unresearched, not as settled. A methodological warning runs through the verification record: several claims' own "supporting quotes" were paraphrases rather than spec text, and WebFetch summarizers twice returned fabricated normative wording, so every quotation in the final deliverable must be re-derived from raw W3C HTML.

findings.claim: WCAG 2.2 adds nine success criteria over 2.1 and removes one (4.1.1 Parsing), giving 87 SCs vs 2.1's 78. The nine and their levels: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) AA, 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) AAA, 2.4.13 Focus Appearance AAA, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements AA, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA, 3.2.6 Consistent Help A, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry A, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) AA, 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) AAA. Six of the nine (2.4.11, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8) are in scope for an A/AA conformance target.
findings.vote: 3-0 (one adjacent phrasing of the same list was voted down 0-3 on quote-support grounds, not on the facts)
findings.evidence: Confirmed against three W3C sources including the normative Recommendation (published 5 Oct 2023, republished 12 Dec 2024). The errata page was checked for supersession: every erratum through 2025-10-28 is Editorial (e.g. "e-mail" -> "email", alphabetizing definitions); none adds, removes, renumbers or renames an SC. Two traps the deliverable must avoid: (a) earlier WCAG 2.2 drafts numbered 2.4.11/2.4.12 as "Focus Appearance (Minimum/Enhanced)" — the final Recommendation uses Focus Not Obscured for 2.4.11/2.4.12 and a single 2.4.13 Focus Appearance; (b) 2.4.7 Focus Visible remains AA, contrary to a common myth that it moved to A. Note the removal of 4.1.1 alongside the nine additions — quoting "adds nine" without it produces a wrong SC count.

findings.claim: SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA, requires a 24x24 CSS pixel effective target area, measured by whether a solid 24x24 CSS px axis-aligned square fits entirely inside the target, with exactly five exceptions: Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential. The Spacing exception is a geometric test — a 24 CSS px diameter circle centered on each undersized target's bounding box must not intersect another target OR the circle for another undersized target — so two adjacent undersized targets need 24px centre-to-centre separation. This makes minimum hit area and inter-target spacing a component/token and layout decision.
findings.vote: 3-0 across five merged claims (0, 5, 7, 10, 11); one narrower restatement of the Spacing test alone was voted 1-2
findings.evidence: Verified by raw curl of the normative spec, not WebFetch summary. Verbatim SC text and all five exception names confirmed; the square-fit measurement rule is verbatim from the Understanding doc's "Size requirement" section but is INFORMATIVE, not normative. Only erratum touching 2.5.8 is 2024-11-19 (#3189), explicitly editorial formatting of the exceptions. Three corrections the deliverable must carry: (1) "hard 24px floor" is imprecise — Spacing permits smaller rendered controls, so the floor is on effective spacing-inclusive activation area, satisfiable by size OR spacing; (2) the Inline exception exempts links inside a sentence and targets constrained by line-height of non-target text, so over-speccing prose links is a real risk; (3) the framing "cannot be retrofitted post-build" is editorially overstated — axe-core ships an automated `target-size` rule (wcag22aa/wcag258, Serious impact) that measures both the size and spacing routes, and padding/min-height remediation is routine. What is genuinely not automatable is the Inline exception (a checker cannot prove line-height constrains the target) and unmarked custom widgets. Cross-platform note for the eventual deliverable: 24 CSS px is web/pointer-scoped; Apple HIG specifies 44x44 pt and Material 48x48 dp, both materially larger, and WCAG's own AAA SC 2.5.5 is 44x44.

findings.claim: SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, Level AA: "All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the functionality is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author." Critically, satisfying the keyboard criteria (2.1.1/2.1.3) does NOT satisfy 2.5.7 — the conforming fix is a pointer-operable control, i.e. a visible affordance that occupies layout space, which is why this is a concept-stage interaction-design decision for author-built reorder lists, kanban boards and map panning.
findings.evidence: Normative text confirmed by raw curl of the 12 Dec 2024 Recommendation; 2.5.7 unaffected by any erratum. W3C's own Understanding examples are exactly the design patterns to spec: "A sortable list of elements may, after tapping or clicking on a list element, provide adjacent controls for moving the element up or down"; "A task board that allows users to drag and drop items between columns also provides an additional pop-up menu after tapping or clicking"; "A map allows users to drag the view of the map around, and the map has up/down/left/right buttons." Understanding also notes there are "very few situations in which dragging movements are essential." TWO SCOPE CORRECTIONS: (a) the claim's original example list over-reached — the user-agent exception means native <input type="range"> and native file-input drop behaviour are exempt; only custom pointer-event sliders and author-built dropzones are in scope, and a drag-to-upload zone usually already ships its alternative as the file input's Browse button; (b) "never a code fix" is not universally true — for a custom slider the conforming alternative is click-anywhere-on-track, a pure implementation change with no new UI. The design-time framing holds specifically for the reorder/kanban/map class W3C itself names. Also do not confuse 2.5.7 with 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (path-based) — one vendor blog claiming touch sliders are exempt as "swipe gestures" makes exactly this error and carries no W3C weight.

findings.claim: Focus obscuring is split across two levels with different thresholds: 2.4.11 (AA) forbids the focused component being ENTIRELY hidden by author-created content — partial obscuring passes at AA — while 2.4.12 (AAA) forbids any part being hidden. 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA) additionally requires a focus indicator at least as large as a 2 CSS px thick perimeter of the component with a 3:1 contrast ratio between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states. W3C names sticky footers, sticky headers and non-modal dialogs as the typical offenders, and cookie banners explicitly, so choosing persistent chrome creates the obligation.
findings.evidence: Normative text verified verbatim in the Recommendation for all three SCs; levels correct (2.4.13 at AAA is a frequent error point — drafts had it at AA). The Understanding doc (page footer "Updated 15 June 2026", i.e. current) states outright "this AA criterion allows for the component receiving focus to be partially obscured" and "Typical types of content that can overlap focused items are sticky footers, sticky headers, and non-modal dialogs" and "A notification implemented as sticky content, such as a cookie banner, will fail this success criterion if it entirely obscures a component receiving focus." W3C ships a dedicated failure technique F110 for sticky footers/headers. FOUR QUALIFIERS: (1) 2.4.11 has two normative notes — only the INITIAL position of user-repositionable content is tested, and content the user opened that can be revealed/dismissed without advancing focus does not count as obscuring; this means a user-opened chat panel can be exempt while a persistent or auto-opening bubble is not, so "floating chat widgets always fail" is wrong. (2) Properly constructed modal dialogs always pass, because they take focus. (3) The 2.4.13 contrast figure is 3:1 between focused and unfocused states of the same pixels, NOT 3:1 against the background — a very easy misquote. (4) W3C explicitly says sticky chrome "can be designed so that they pass", so the honest framing is that the overlay decision creates a paired obligation, not that sticky headers fail.

findings.claim: For cookie banners and similar sticky notifications W3C names concrete passing designs decided at design time: make the banner modal so it must be dismissed before navigating the page, or use CSS scroll-padding so the banner never overlaps other content. A third named option is closing notifications on loss of focus. Scroll-padding is a formally listed Sufficient Technique (C43), not just prose advice.
findings.evidence: Verbatim from the live Understanding page: "Ways of passing include making the banner modal so the user has to dismiss the banner before navigating through the page, or using scroll padding so the banner does not overlap other content." Corroborated in the same document's Examples section by both a full-width modal cookie dialog and a sticky-footer-plus-scroll-padding case, and formalized as Sufficient Technique C43 with F110 as the matching failure. TWO QUALIFIERS: the list is explicitly open ("Ways of passing include") and the very next sentence names a third route — "Notifications that do not require user action could also meet this criterion by closing on loss of focus" — so do not present two as exhaustive. Understanding docs are labelled informative; normative force here comes from the SC text plus C43. Of the three, only modal-vs-non-modal is a pure concept-time decision; scroll-padding's design-time counterpart is "reserve layout space for persistent sticky chrome."

findings.claim: SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), Level AA: a cognitive function test is not required for any step in an authentication process unless that step provides at least one of exactly four exceptions — Alternative (another method not relying on a cognitive function test), Mechanism (something assists the user in completing the test), Object Recognition, or Personal Content. The AAA sibling 3.3.9 keeps only Alternative and Mechanism. Supporting password managers and permitting copy-paste into username/password fields is the accepted way to satisfy Mechanism — and it is named in the NORMATIVE Note 2, not just guidance.
findings.vote: 3-0 across merged claims 12 and 13 (two looser paraphrases of the same SC were voted 0-3 for misstating the exception set)
findings.evidence: Verified against raw HTML of the 12 Dec 2024 Recommendation. Normative Note 2 reads: "Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by password managers to reduce memory need, and copy and paste to reduce the cognitive burden of re-typing." The mechanism definition explicitly permits relying on the platform or user agent rather than building it: "The mechanism may be explicitly provided in the content, or may be relied upon to be provided by either the platform or by user agents, including assistive technologies." Only erratum touching 3.3.8 is #18 (2024-11-19), changing ordered lists to unordered — pure formatting. IMPORTANT PARAPHRASE TRAP: the SC says a cognitive function test "is not required", it does not forbid offering one — W3C's own Understanding page states it "does not forbid cognitive function tests outright." Writing "3.3.8 bans password fields" is a misreading; the Alternative exception is precisely what converts required into not-required. Two claims in the source set that stated the exceptions as "unless essential" or listed only object-recognition and personal-content were refuted 0-3 — there is no essentiality/security exception in 3.3.8. One verifier also caught a WebFetch summarizer inventing the wording "except where that test is essential to the security of the content", which appears nowhere in the spec.

findings.claim: Actively blocking password managers from filling login fields, or blocking copy-and-paste, is a W3C-stated failure of 3.3.8 unless an alternative is provided — so the common security-team decision to disable paste on password fields is itself the accessibility defect. Requiring a password or code to be re-entered in a different format from the one it was created in (split OTP boxes, "enter the 2nd, 6th and last characters") is failure technique F109.
findings.evidence: Verbatim from the Understanding page: "if user agents and password managers are actively blocked from filling in the fields (for instance, by a script that prevents form fields from being automatically populated), or users are prevented from copy and paste operations (as they may rely on standalone/external third party password managers), then the page would fail this criterion unless an alternative is provided." F109 (revised 27 April 2026, current) covers the format-change case and states "A service that requires manual transcription of a verification code is not compliant." ADVERSARIAL HISTORY WORTH KNOWING: w3c/wcag issue #1855 (Patrick Lauke, 2021) empirically showed across Win/mac/iOS/Android x four browsers x five password managers that "None of the tested combinations generate/trigger a paste event" — i.e. blocking paste does not actually block extension-based managers. Alastair Campbell conceded the point; the issue was closed via PR #1898 and the published text was rewritten to justify the paste clause independently (users of standalone/external managers). So the strongest counter-argument was adjudicated and folded in, not ignored. TWO QUALIFIERS: the failure is conditional on "unless an alternative is provided" — a site offering passkeys/WebAuthn or an email magic link alongside still conforms, which is why the alternative-method decision is architectural; and this specific case lives in the informative Understanding doc, so the accurate formulation is "W3C states this is a failure" rather than "the SC text names it."

findings.claim: SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry is Level A — the lowest tier, not AA. Normative text: information previously entered by or provided to the user that is required to be entered again IN THE SAME PROCESS is either auto-populated or available for the user to select. Three exceptions: re-entering is essential, the information is required to ensure security of the content, or the previously entered information is no longer valid. This pushes multi-step flow and checkout design toward auto-population or offering prior values.
findings.vote: 2-1 (the dissent was on quote fidelity, not substance)
findings.evidence: Level A confirmed by both the Understanding heading and the WAI What's New page; every secondary source located independently agrees. THREE CORRECTIONS: (1) the claim's supplied quote is a paraphrase — the normative disjunction is "either: auto-populated, or available for the user to select", which maps exactly onto the design implication; (2) the claim named only two of three exceptions, dropping "previously entered information is no longer valid"; (3) the claim dropped the normative scoping "in the same process" (W3C defines process as a sequence of activities toward one goal). W3C's own plain-language summary loosely says "same session", which is looser than normative text — without "same process" a reader could over-apply this across unrelated visits. Open W3C issues (w3c/wcag #1660, #4210) debate how the security exception applies to password re-entry; that is edge-case interpretation, not a dispute about the level or the core requirement.

findings.claim: WCAG 3.0 is a W3C Working Draft dated 3 March 2026 whose own text states "it still has several years of work", it explicitly does not deprecate WCAG 2 ("WCAG 2 is used around the world and will still be required by different countries for a long time to come"), and WCAG 2.2 A+AA conformance is only "expected to meet MOST of the minimum conformance level" because WCAG 3 adds tests and different scoring mechanics. No 2026 design or procurement decision can be anchored to WCAG 3 conformance; WCAG 2.2 AA is the operative design target.
findings.evidence: All three quotes verified verbatim in the live 3 March 2026 Working Draft; publication history checked April-July 2026 and no newer draft exists as of 28 July 2026. The draft self-labels "It is inappropriate to cite this document as other than a work in progress", which independently supports the procurement inference. WAI's WCAG 3 intro page corroborates: "WCAG 3 will not supersede WCAG 2 and WCAG 2 will not be deprecated for at least several years after WCAG 3 is finalized." THREE CAVEATS: (1) the March 2026 Conformance section does NOT itself name levels — it says only "several levels of conformance are available" and carries an editor's note that the conformance model was updated with open questions; the Bronze/Silver/Gold naming comes from prior drafts and secondary commentary, so the intro's phrase "different scoring mechanics" currently outruns the draft's own normative text. (2) The Working Group was chartered only through April 2026; secondary trackers put CR around Q4 2027 and REC no earlier than 2028. (3) "WCAG 2.2 is the operative target" is inference, not W3C wording — no major jurisdiction legally mandates 2.2 today. State it as "2.2 is the right design target; 2.1 AA is what the law currently names."

findings.claim: Every legal instrument currently in force points at WCAG 2.x, never WCAG 3: DOJ's ADA Title II rule (28 CFR part 35 subpart H, 89 FR 31320, 24 Apr 2024) adopts WCAG 2.1 Level AA, and a DOJ interim final rule published 20 April 2026 pushed compliance dates from 24 Apr 2026 to 26 April 2027 for entities of 50,000+ population and from 26 Apr 2027 to 26 April 2028 for smaller entities and special districts. EN 301 549 v3.2.1 — the harmonised standard cited for the European Accessibility Act, applicable 28 June 2025 — incorporates WCAG 2.1, with v4.1.1 moving to WCAG 2.2 AA anticipated in the OJEU around October 2026. Section 508 still references WCAG 2.0 AA.
findings.vote: not independently voted — surfaced as corroborating evidence inside the 3-0 verifications of claims 17 and 18
findings.evidence: This material was gathered by two verifiers while checking whether WCAG 3 had displaced WCAG 2 in any binding instrument; both independently reported the same dates and citations, and it is internally consistent across them. It is downgraded to MEDIUM because it was never itself put through the three-vote adversarial process, the Federal Register and ETSI URLs above are reconstructed from the verifiers' prose rather than fetched during synthesis, and the EN 301 549 v4.1.1 OJEU date is forward-looking. The load-bearing conclusion — that no in-force law names WCAG 3, and that the design target gap between the legally named 2.1 and the current 2.2 Recommendation is exactly the nine new SCs minus 4.1.1 — is solid. The specific dates and CFR/FR citations MUST be re-verified against the primary texts before any deliverable states them. The DOJ deadline extension in particular is recent and consequential enough that a stale figure would be actively misleading.

findings.claim: SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help is Level A, but nothing beyond its level and existence survived verification — its normative requirement, the help mechanisms it covers, and its design implications were never independently checked.
findings.vote: level established only as a by-product of the 3-0 verification of the nine-SC list (claim 4)
findings.evidence: 3.2.6 appears in the verified nine-SC index at Level A and in the WAI What's New level table, and a 2025 erratum touching 3.2.6 was noted in passing on the errata page. No claim in the surviving set states what 3.2.6 actually requires (consistent relative order of help mechanisms across pages in a set of web pages), what counts as a help mechanism, or what it demands of a designer — which was an explicit ask in the brief. Treat this as a research gap, not a finding. Anyone writing the deliverable must fetch https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html directly.

findings.claim: Methodological warning that affects the whole deliverable: WebFetch-style summarization repeatedly returned FABRICATED normative text for WCAG success criteria, and several of the research claims' own "supporting quotes" turned out to be paraphrases that do not appear anywhere in the spec. Every quotation must be re-derived from raw W3C HTML (curl / raw.githubusercontent.com/w3c/wcag) before publication.
findings.vote: 3-0 equivalent — independently reported by verifiers of claims 0, 1, 3, 10 and 12
findings.evidence: Concrete instances caught: (a) for 2.5.8 a summarizer returned "A larger alternative target serving the same purpose and function is available" and "The target is an element in a continuous paragraph of text" — neither is W3C wording; (b) for 3.3.8 a summarizer invented "not required to authenticate a user, except where that test is essential to the security of the content", which appears nowhere in the spec and would have introduced a non-existent security exception; (c) the supplied supporting quotes for the 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.3.7 and 3.3.8 claims were all paraphrases, one of which conflated the Spacing and Inline exceptions of 2.5.8 into a single sentence that does not exist. Verifiers that used curl on the TR document or the w3c/wcag raw source got clean text every time. For a document whose value is quoting a standard accurately, this is the single highest-risk failure mode.

result.caveats:
COVERAGE IS THE BIGGEST CAVEAT. Of the eight areas requested, only two are actually evidenced. All 20 surviving claims concern WCAG 2.2's new success criteria (area 1) and WCAG 3.0's status (area 2). NOTHING survived verification on: the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide and the "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" rule (area 3); focus management on route change and view transitions in SPAs (area 4); live regions / aria-live failure modes across screen readers (area 5); accessible names for custom controls (area 6); the legal drivers in any detail — EAA, DOJ Title II, Section 508, EN 301 549 (area 7, partially covered only as incidental corroboration at medium confidence); and native iOS VoiceOver/Dynamic Type/traits vs Android TalkBack (area 8). These are unresearched, not settled. Do not let the depth on WCAG 2.2 imply the rest was checked.

SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help was in the brief's explicit list and is effectively unresearched beyond its Level A designation.

QUOTE INTEGRITY. Several claims carried "supporting quotes" that are paraphrases absent from the spec, and summarizer tools twice produced fabricated normative text including a non-existent security exception for 3.3.8. Nothing in the final deliverable should be quoted from this report without re-fetching raw W3C HTML.

FRAMING vs FACT. The recurring tail clause "this is a design-time decision, not a post-build audit item" is the brief's editorial framing, never W3C text, and is factually wrong in places: axe-core automates 2.5.8 detection, target size is routinely remediated with CSS padding, and the 2.5.7 fix for a custom slider is a pure implementation change. The defensible version is narrower — these criteria are cheapest and most reliably satisfied when decided in the comp, and several (equivalent-control IA, non-drag affordances, sticky-chrome geometry, auth method choice) require new UI or new architecture that cannot be bolted on.

INFORMATIVE vs NORMATIVE. Much of the most designer-useful material (the square-fit rule for 2.5.8, the sticky-header/cookie-banner naming, the paste-blocking failure case) lives in Understanding documents, which are explicitly labelled "Informative explanations, not required to meet WCAG." Attribute it as "W3C guidance states" rather than "the criterion requires."

TIME SENSITIVITY. WCAG 2.2 is stable — errata through 2025-10-28 are all editorial. WCAG 3.0 is not: the March 2026 draft's conformance model has open editor's questions, the Working Group's charter ran to April 2026, and any level naming (Bronze/Silver/Gold) is from older drafts. The legal timeline is the most volatile element here — DOJ deadlines moved in April 2026 and EN 301 549 v4.1.1 is expected in the OJEU around October 2026; re-verify all dates at time of writing.

PLATFORM SCOPE. Every number in this report is web/CSS-pixel scoped. Verifiers flagged in passing that Apple HIG (44x44 pt) and Material (48x48 dp) specify materially larger touch targets, so no WCAG figure transfers to native without restating it.
openQuestions: What does SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help actually require — what counts as a help mechanism, what "same relative order" means across a set of web pages, and what it forces a designer to decide about global nav and footer placement? It was in the brief and only its Level A designation was established.

Areas 3-6 of the brief (ARIA APG patterns as design decisions, the "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" rule with concrete wrong-answer cases, SPA route-change focus management and the View Transitions API, aria-live failure modes across NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver, and accessible-name computation for custom controls) produced zero verified claims. Was this a scoping decision by the research pass, or did those claims fail verification? They need a dedicated research round against W3C ARIA APG, WAI-ARIA 1.2/1.3, and screen-reader support tables.

How do the native platforms map onto these web criteria — does Apple's 44x44 pt / Material's 48x48 dp guidance satisfy or exceed 2.5.8 in a legal sense under EN 301 549 clauses 11.x, and what are the iOS/Android equivalents of 2.5.7 (drag alternatives), 2.4.11 (focus obscuring under sticky nav bars) and 3.3.8 (biometric/passkey auth as the Alternative exception)?

Which of the nine new WCAG 2.2 criteria are actually enforceable today, given that DOJ Title II names WCAG 2.1 AA and Section 508 names 2.0 AA — i.e. is designing to 2.2 a legal requirement anywhere in 2026, or purely anticipatory of EN 301 549 v4.1.1? The report establishes that 2.2 is not currently mandated but does not resolve whether any procurement regime already requires it.

Does the 2.4.11 note exempting user-opened dismissible content extend to the common pattern of an auto-opening chat widget that the user can close, or only to content the user explicitly invoked? This determines whether a very widespread commercial pattern conforms.
